Meridian AI should have access to the complete source of the **exact installed Meridian revision**.

This includes, where available:

- implementation;
- documentation;
- tests;
- benchmarks;
- examples;
- architectural notes;
- source-control history;
- previous relevant fixes.

Stable Meridian knowledge should be heavily trained into TemperTally.

Version-specific or potentially changed facts should prefer the installed source as authoritative.

The model should not trust its parametric memory over current engine source when those disagree.

---

### AI 20. Agent-computer interface `AI-009`

> **Identifier provenance.** `AI-009` — *Typed Meridian agent-computer interface and deep observability*, locked in planning ledger v0.66 and restored here. The concept survived synthesis as AI 20–23; the stable identifier did not. The sequential `AI N.` numbering in this section is prose ordering and is **not** equivalent to the `AI-0NN` requirement family.

The model should interact primarily with **typed Meridian APIs**, not scrape human-facing CLI output.

Preferred domains include:

```text
source
scene
world
physics
render
audio
animation
assets
MUI
build
test
debug
profile
package
dependencies
source_control
runtime

```

Results should be concise, structured, expandable, and provenance-aware.

If Meridian already understands information structurally, the model should receive it structurally.

---

The AI should eventually be able to inspect:

- render graph;
- render passes;
- dependencies;
- GPU timings;
- resources;
- pipelines;

- shader IR;

This allows questions such as:

to be answered using actual engine state rather than screenshot speculation.

### AI 22. Rich physics integration

The agent should be able to inspect:

- bodies;

### AI 23. Debugging and observability

Meridian AI should receive substantially richer debugging information than a generic coding agent.

The AI should eventually be able to ask:

> Who last wrote this value?

> Which system caused this allocation?

> Why is this object still alive?

### AI 24. Experiments `AI-010`

> **Identifier provenance.** `AI-010` — *Experiments and Branch-and-Verify*, locked in planning ledger v0.66 and restored here. The concept survived synthesis as AI 24–25; the stable identifier did not. The sequential `AI N.` numbering in this section is prose ordering and is **not** equivalent to the `AI-0NN` requirement family.

Experiments should be first-class objects.

Conceptually:

```text
Experiment {
    hypothesis
    environment
    modifications
    measurements
    repetitions
    result
    artifacts
}
```

The AI should be able to create isolated temporary experiments rather than repeatedly mutate the live project.

Experiments may include:

- randomized physics simulations;
- alternative renderer implementations;
- asset compression comparisons;
- performance benchmarks;
- UI alternatives;
- code implementation variants.

---

### AI 25. Branch-and-Verify

Where multiple solutions are plausible, the harness should be able to create isolated Meridian snapshots/transactions and evaluate them independently.

Example:

```text
A
implement
compile
test
benchmark

B
implement
compile
test
benchmark

C
implement
compile
test
→ failed
```

Then select the best verified result.

Previous planning reserved **Branch-and-Verify** as a research anchor for this behavior.

This must not rely on direct Git usage.

---

### AI 26. No direct Git access `AI-011`

> **Identifier provenance.** `AI-011` — *No raw Git, brokered processes, no irreversible destruction*, locked in planning ledger v0.66 and restored here. The concept survived synthesis as AI 26–28; the stable identifier did not. The sequential `AI N.` numbering in this section is prose ordering and is **not** equivalent to the `AI-0NN` requirement family.

**Agents never use Git directly.**

This includes read-only usage.

Agents must not invoke:

```text
git status
git diff
git commit
git reset
git push
```

and must not bypass the restriction through:

- Python libraries;
- libgit;
- shell aliases;
- direct `.git` mutation.

All source-control operations go through Meridian’s own source-control APIs and abstractions.

Conceptually:

```text
source_control.status
source_control.diff
source_control.history
source_control.inspect_change
source_control.checkpoint
source_control.restore
source_control.create_change
source_control.merge
source_control.prepare_publish
```

Meridian’s backend may remain Git-compatible and use Meridian’s planned jj-derived source-control architecture.

The AI operates on **Meridian semantics**, not Git semantics.

---

### AI 27. Process execution

External tools remain necessary, but arbitrary process execution must be brokered by Meridian.

The process API should understand:

- filesystem scope;
- network scope;
- environment filtering;
- resource limits;
- protected paths;
- timeouts;
- credentials;
- provenance.

Common work should use first-party structured APIs instead of raw shell commands where possible.

For example:

```text
build.run()
test.run()
dependencies.add()
profile.capture()
package.build()
```

---

### AI 28. No destructive agent operations

Agents must not perform irreversible destructive tasks.

This is an architectural boundary, not merely a classifier preference.

A project file may be removed through a reversible transaction.

That is different from irreversible destruction.

Example:

```text
remove obsolete.rs

→ checkpoint
→ transactional removal
→ recoverable
```

The AI cannot permanently purge recovery history.

Agent capabilities must not include operations such as:

- permanent arbitrary data destruction;
- irreversible source-control history destruction;
- deleting remote repositories;
- destroying production infrastructure;
- wiping backups;
- disabling its own safety system.

There is no Meridian equivalent of:

```text
--dangerously-skip-permissions
```

---

### AI 29. Action Governor `AI-012`

> **Identifier provenance.** `AI-012` — *Action Governor and trust-boundary model*, locked in planning ledger v0.66 and restored here. The concept survived synthesis as AI 29–30; the stable identifier did not. The sequential `AI N.` numbering in this section is prose ordering and is **not** equivalent to the `AI-0NN` requirement family.

**Current locked external-action policy:** scoped reversible private remote actions may be preauthorized. Publication, merge, release, deployment, store submission, external messaging, permission/credential/billing changes, destructive remote deletion and making data public require explicit human final authorization. Preparing the complete artifact/draft is allowed; crossing the public/irreversible boundary is not.

The harness should contain a separate action-governance system.

The model proposes **typed operations**.

The governor evaluates known effects.

Conceptually:

```text
Proposed action
      │
      ▼
Hard capability check
      │
      ├─ prohibited → BLOCK
      │
      ▼
Deterministic effect policy
      │
      ├─ trivially safe → ALLOW
      │
      ▼
Intent classifier
   ┌──┼──┐
ALLOW ASK BLOCK
```

Possible action metadata includes:

```text
scope
mutates_state
reversible
external
publishes_data
uses_credentials
affects_remote_state
cost
network_destination
source_control_effect
self_configuration_effect
```

The governor should not receive the main model’s persuasive reasoning about why its own proposed action is safe.

It should primarily receive:

- hard policy;
- raw user instruction;
- applicable `AGENTS.md`;
- trusted Meridian state;
- active task constraints;
- typed proposed action.

---

### AI 30. Prompt-injection handling

Retrieved content must have provenance.

Examples:

```text
SYSTEM
USER
MERIDIAN_TRUSTED
PROJECT
DEPENDENCY
EXTERNAL
UNTRUSTED
```

External documentation, webpages, dependency code, issue text, or other untrusted information must not gain policy authority merely because the model read it.

Prompt-injection detection should be separate from action approval.

Hard structural capability limits remain the strongest defense.

---

### AI 31. `AGENTS.md` `AI-013`

> **Identifier provenance.** `AI-013` — *`AGENTS.md`, `.meridian/`, skills and instruction precedence*, locked in planning ledger v0.66 and restored here. The concept survived synthesis as AI 31–35; the stable identifier did not. The sequential `AI N.` numbering in this section is prose ordering and is **not** equivalent to the `AI-0NN` requirement family.

Every Meridian repository has:

```text
AGENTS.md
```

**at the repository root. Always.**

This is the primary portable human-readable agent instruction file.

Nested `AGENTS.md` files should **not** be routine.

A nested file is created only when a particular folder/subtree genuinely requires specialized scoped instructions.

Example:

```text
repo/
├── AGENTS.md
├── src/
│   ├── physics/
│   │   └── AGENTS.md    # only if physics requires unique rules
│   └── render/
└── .meridian/
```

Do not generate one for every crate or directory.

---

### AI 32. `AGENTS.md` precedence

Conceptually:

```text
Hard Meridian invariants
        ↓
User security/capability policy
        ↓
Current explicit user instruction
        ↓
Nearest applicable scoped AGENTS.md
        ↓
Root AGENTS.md
        ↓
Structured Meridian project configuration
        ↓
skills/defaults
```

`AGENTS.md` cannot grant authority the agent does not possess.

Because `AGENTS.md` is high-authority project guidance, Meridian AI should not casually rewrite it.

It may:

- read it automatically;
- propose changes;
- update it when explicitly instructed;
- ask to promote a repeatedly corrected rule into it.

It should not silently convert every user preference into permanent root policy.

---

### AI 33. `.meridian/`

`.meridian/` stores structured Meridian-specific configuration/state.

Conceptually it may contain:

- project configuration;
- AI configuration;
- skills;
- plans;
- tasks;
- local indexes;
- traces;
- memory;
- cache metadata;
- extension metadata;
- provider information;
- training configuration.

The exact internal layout is **not yet frozen**.

`AGENTS.md` and `.meridian/` have different roles:

> `AGENTS.md` = portable human-readable agent guidance.

> `.meridian/` = structured Meridian machine state/configuration.

---

### AI 34. Skills

Skills are dynamically loadable procedural capabilities.

A skill may contain:

- concise model instructions;
- procedures;
- relevant Meridian capabilities;
- retrieval presets;
- verification requirements;
- examples;
- optional native implementation.

Skills should be loaded when relevant instead of occupying permanent context.

Meridian AI may create a project skill when it detects a useful recurring workflow.

Skills must never expand authority.

Formally:

```text
Capabilities(skill)
⊆
Capabilities(parent task)
```

---

### AI 35. Skill lifecycle

Self-created skills should not immediately be trusted as highly as first-party Meridian skills.

A conceptual lifecycle is:

```text
DRAFT
PROVEN
TRUSTED
STALE
DISABLED
```

A skill can become stale when:

- Meridian APIs change;
- the project architecture changes;
- verification begins failing.

The harness should automatically detect this where possible.

---

### AI 36. Self-configuration `AI-014`

> **Identifier provenance.** `AI-014` — *Resource-aware self-configuration without self-escalation*, locked in planning ledger v0.66 and restored here. The concept survived synthesis as AI 36–38; the stable identifier did not. The sequential `AI N.` numbering in this section is prose ordering and is **not** equivalent to the `AI-0NN` requirement family.

Meridian AI should understand and configure its own harness.

It should know:

- current model;
- available models;
- provider;
- context capacity;
- active context;
- available skills;
- retrieval state;
- indexing state;
- memory pressure;
- inference performance;
- subagent concurrency;
- cache state;
- reasoning budget;
- provider cost policy.

Safe operational configuration should normally be performed directly.

Examples:

```text
increase context
increase retrieval depth
change reranking budget
rebuild index
enable trusted skill
reduce subagents under memory pressure
change local cache strategy
increase reasoning effort
switch approved local model
```

It should not merely tell the user where the setting is.

---

### AI 37. Self-configuration is not self-escalation

The model can make itself more efficient.

It cannot make itself more authorized.

```text
new capabilities
⊆
existing authorized capabilities
```

There is no agent-accessible function for:

```text
disable_governor()
allow_destructive_actions()
remove_human_review()
grant_arbitrary_filesystem_access()
```

A skill, subagent, provider, model switch, project file, or external instruction cannot change this.

---

### AI 38. Resource Director

A resource-management subsystem should automatically adapt AI execution to the current machine.

It should know:

- available RAM;
- VRAM/unified memory;
- memory pressure;
- CPU/GPU/NPU capability;
- SSD throughput;
- active KV state;
- editor/game workload;
- battery/power where useful;
- third-party API cost.

This system decides:

- context allocation;
- subagent concurrency;
- KV residency;
- SSD paging;
- model routing;
- cache strategy;
- whether expensive parallel work is worthwhile.

Normal users should not need to configure these manually.

---

### AI 39. Subagents `AI-015`

> **Identifier provenance.** `AI-015` — *Sparse subagents over shared weights*, locked in planning ledger v0.66 and restored here. The concept survived synthesis as AI 39–42; the stable identifier did not. The sequential `AI N.` numbering in this section is prose ordering and is **not** equivalent to the `AI-0NN` requirement family.

Subagents are supported, but should not become the default answer to difficult work.

Default:

```text
one strong primary agent
+
excellent tools
```

Subagents are justified for:

- isolated investigation;
- independent verification;
- genuinely parallel hypotheses;
- separate context-heavy research;
- competing implementation experiments.

The primary agent remains responsible for:

- the user relationship;
- task interpretation;
- integrating findings;
- questions;
- final result.

Workers should normally never talk directly to the user.

---

### AI 40. Logical local subagents

Local subagents should not require loading multiple copies of TemperTally.

TQF should support multiple logical contexts over one model weight set:

```text
            TemperTally weights
                     │
       ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
       │             │             │
    main KV       debug KV      verifier KV
```

Potential runtime optimizations include:

- shared immutable prefixes;
- copy-on-write context forks;
- KV paging;
- expert residency reuse;
- batched inference;
- inactive-context eviction;
- SSD-backed cold contexts.

On memory-constrained systems, workers can execute sequentially.

On larger systems, they may run concurrently.

Cloud/frontier models can parallelize more aggressively.

---

### AI 41. Worker composition

Do not create hundreds of fixed AI personalities.

Conceptually use:

```text
role × domain × skill
```

Example:

```text
role: Debugger
domain: Physics
skills:
- constraint analysis
- simulation replay
```

Potential roles include:

- exploration;
- planning;
- implementation;
- debugging;
- verification;
- performance;
- external research;
- review.

The exact taxonomy is not frozen.

---

### AI 42. Worker output

Workers should return structured findings rather than essays.

Conceptually:

```text
Finding {
    claim
    evidence
    uncertainty
    affected_systems
    suggested_actions
    artifacts
    unresolved_questions
}
```

The full raw worker trace remains available externally.

The primary agent receives the compact finding.

### AI 43. Planning architecture `AI-016`

> **Identifier provenance.** `AI-016` — *Adaptive planning, no-change outcomes and verification*, locked in planning ledger v0.66 and restored here. The concept survived synthesis as AI 43–46; the stable identifier did not. The sequential `AI N.` numbering in this section is prose ordering and is **not** equivalent to the `AI-0NN` requirement family.

Planning should scale with task complexity.

Tiny task:

```text
understand → edit → verify
```

Normal bug:

```text
reproduce → diagnose → repair → verify
```

Large feature:

```text
persistent dependency-aware implementation plan
```

Plans should track:

- goal;
- constraints;
- assumptions;
- decisions;
- dependencies;
- implementation nodes;
- completion criteria;
- verification requirements;
- current status.

Plans must mutate when evidence changes.

---

### AI 44. No-change is a valid result

TemperTally must be explicitly trained not to manufacture changes merely because a user reported a problem.

Valid resolutions include:

```text
CODE CHANGE
CONFIGURATION CHANGE
REBUILD
EXPLANATION
ENGINE EXTENSION
NO CHANGE REQUIRED
```

Examples:

- the issue is already fixed;
- stale assets were running;
- the user misunderstood expected behavior;
- the reported bug cannot be reproduced;
- the correct fix is an existing setting.

“Produces a diff” must not be treated as synonymous with success.

---

### AI 45. Verification

Verification should rely on deterministic evidence whenever possible.

Possible verifiers include:

- Rust compiler;
- language compilers;
- type checkers;
- tests;
- integration tests;
- shader compiler;
- scene validator;
- simulation;
- replay;
- renderer comparison;
- profiler;
- benchmarks;
- sanitizers;
- asset checks;
- platform builds.

The model’s self-confidence is not verification.

---

### AI 46. Evidence contracts

Large plan nodes should be able to define what evidence is required before being considered verified.

Example:

```text
Fix gravity handoff

Required:
✓ issue no longer reproduces
✓ movement regression tests pass
✓ maximum intended velocity behavior unchanged
✓ physics benchmark remains within budget
```

The harness, not the model, decides whether those evidence slots actually exist.

---

### AI 47. Meridian engine limitations `AI-017`

> **Identifier provenance.** `AI-017` — *Engine-limit extensions and mandatory-reviewed upstream issue publication*, locked in planning ledger v0.66 and restored here. The concept survived synthesis as AI 47–49; the stable identifier did not. The sequential `AI N.` numbering in this section is prose ordering and is **not** equivalent to the `AI-0NN` requirement family.

If the agent determines that the user’s desired result is blocked by a **genuine Meridian limitation**, it should not immediately write a brittle project hack.

The preferred workflow is:

```text
Investigate
    ↓
Prove Meridian limitation
    ↓
Check existing extension/API path
    ↓
Author scoped Meridian extension
    ↓
Validate extension
    ↓
Use extension as temporary project workaround
    ↓
Prepare upstream Meridian issue
    ↓
MANDATORY HUMAN REVIEW
```

---

### AI 48. Temporary Meridian extensions

A generated extension should:

- be scoped;
- use proper Meridian extension APIs;
- avoid patching installed engine internals;
- include tests;
- include provenance;
- document the engine limitation;
- record the Meridian revision;
- record why the extension exists;
- define a native-replacement condition where possible.

Conceptually:

```text
Temporary workaround

Reason:
Meridian lacks feature X.

Extension:
RegionAtmosphere

Required since:
Meridian revision ABC

Replacement condition:
Native equivalent becomes available.
```

If a later Meridian version gains the missing capability, Meridian AI should:

1. detect the overlap;
2. test the native implementation;
3. propose migration;
4. safely remove the temporary extension if successful.

---

### AI 49. Upstream Meridian issue preparation

When a genuine Meridian limitation or bug is found, the AI may:

- reproduce it;
- minimize it;
- inspect source;
- collect diagnostics;
- search existing issues;
- deduplicate;
- prepare a high-quality report;
- include relevant extension/reference implementation information;
- sanitize private project details;
- open the completed draft in Meridian’s review interface.

It **may never publish the GitHub issue automatically**.

Ever.

Issue publication requires:

> **human review + explicit human submission**

There is no configuration, provider, permission mode, skill, or model capable of bypassing this rule.

---

### AI 50. AI Control Plane

The Control Plane exposes safe harness configuration to models.

Possible domains:

```text
models
providers
context
reasoning
retrieval
skills
workers
memory
resource policy
network policy
verification
diagnostics
```

Every setting should carry autonomy metadata.

Examples:

### Safe ephemeral

- retrieval depth;
- active context;
- local cache policy;
- reasoning effort.

May be changed automatically.

### Safe persistent

- trusted skill activation;
- project indexing.

May usually change automatically and remain visible in settings/history.

### Cost/privacy boundary

- switching to a cloud model;
- transmitting project source;
- substantially increasing API usage.

Requires preauthorization or a question.

### Security authority

- destructive permissions;
- hard policy;
- mandatory human boundaries.

Not agent-modifiable.

---

### AI 51. Provider capability negotiation

Each provider/model advertises capabilities.

Conceptually:

```text
ModelProfile {
    context_length
    vision
    tool_calling
    structured_output
    reasoning_controls
    parallel_requests
    prompt_cache
    local_or_cloud
    privacy
    pricing
    Meridian_native_features
}
```

The harness adapts itself rather than assuming every model works like an OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint.

### AI 52. Meridian-native action representation

Meridian should investigate a compact typed model-native action representation, previously referred to as **MAIR**.

The goals are:

- fewer tokens than verbose JSON;
- deterministic parsing;
- typed operations;
- strong reinforcement-training suitability;
- efficient TQF generation;
- ordinary tool adapters for third-party models.

This remains a research direction, not a finalized language or syntax. Prior Meridian planning explicitly reserved a compact typed deterministic Meridian-native action representation while leaving its exact syntax and architecture open.

### AI 56. Expert specialization

Do not manually designate:

```text
Expert 12 = Rust
Expert 84 = Physics
Expert 121 = TypeScript
```

The correct process is:

1. profile Qwen’s natural expert routing;
2. perform Meridian specialization;
3. profile routing again;
4. identify stable emergent expert communities;
5. strengthen useful specialization where it improves results.

Previous planning used **ExpertGuild** as a research anchor for soft/emergent expert specialization rather than fixed assignment.

### AI 57. Expert pruning and model slimming

Once TemperTally Full is strong, build a parameter-efficiency frontier.

Example research candidates:

```text
35B
27B
22B
19B
17B
15B
14B
13B
11B
```

Do not prune before measuring what Meridian specialization actually did to routing.

Explore:

- expert removal;
- nonuniform expert retention per layer;
- expert merging;
- expert-width slimming;
- neuron-level pruning;
- router retraining;
- active top-k reduction.

Total-parameter pruning and active-compute reduction are different problems and must be measured separately.

---

### AI 58. Main compressed-model target

A particularly attractive research target is approximately:

> **12–16B total parameters / ~2B active**

with approximately **14B / ~2B active** as a useful central experiment.

This is a target, not a promise.

The final model size should be chosen empirically from:

```text
MeridianBench quality
vs
RAM
vs
disk
vs
tokens/sec
vs
energy
```

The user should not see a zoo of technical model variants unless there is a real product reason.

There should remain one obvious recommended:

> **TemperTally**

---

### AI 59. Dense distillation

In parallel with the main sparse model, attempt to distill TemperTally Full into approximately:

> **4–7B dense parameters**

This may become:

- a compact fallback;
- a fast low-memory variant;
- a research model;
- potentially a cheap internal task model.

It should not automatically become another user-facing edition.

Benchmark first.

If it is not useful, do not ship it.

---

### AI 60. Quantization

The main shipping TemperTally should target approximately **Q5-quality storage**.

This should not mean every tensor is exactly five bits.

Use Meridian-specific sensitivity calibration.

Conceptually:

```text
very sensitive tensors
→ BF16 / FP16 / INT8 / Q6

important attention/model tensors
→ Q6-ish

most retained expert tensors
→ Q5-ish

highly tolerant tensors
→ Q4-ish
```

The resulting model may average approximately **5–5.3 bits per weight**.

Quantization calibration data must contain Meridian workloads, not generic text alone.

---

### AI 61. Training precision vs deployment precision

Do not train the canonical model by repeatedly quantizing a Q5 checkpoint.

Maintain the best high-quality internal model in appropriately high precision.

Use low-memory training techniques to train from consumer hardware while preserving adequate compute precision.

Possible strategies include:

- frozen quantized base + higher-precision adapters;
- selective expert training;
- router-only training;
- low-rank updates;
- gradient projection;
- structured optimizer-state compression;
- temporary promotion of trainable tensors to higher precision.

Final deployment quantization is generated from the best high-quality checkpoint.

---

### AI 62. Runtime quality requirement

Compression, paging, KV optimization, quantization, retrieval optimization, and other TQF techniques must be evaluated against model quality.

The previously established TQF direction is to keep **measured quality degradation at or below approximately 1%** for aggressive runtime optimizations where possible.

Do not create user-facing “bad quality but tiny RAM” modes to paper over major degradation.

Autotune instead.

### AI 65. Training philosophy

TemperTally should not be built by brute-force foundation-model retraining.

The project is designed around **compute leverage**.

Use:

```text
excellent base model
+
frontier teachers
+
verified synthetic data
+
Meridian environment execution
+
selective training
+
SSD-backed low-memory training
+
distillation
+
pruning/slimming
+
aggressive evaluation
```

The system must be practical for a solo developer who is comfortable allowing personal computers to train continuously for days.

### AI 76. Teacher ensemble

Conceptually:

```text

                  │
        ┌─────────┼─────────┐
        │         │         │

        │         │         │
        └─────────┼─────────┘

                  │
                  ▼

                  │
```

### AI 76A. GPT-5.6 Luna teacher use

GPT-5.6 Luna is a planned primary frontier teacher. Its role is determined by verified task quality and cost rather than brand preference. Use it for difficult planning, coding, tool-use, critique, long-context and synthetic-curriculum generation where it performs well under Meridian verification. Do not encode vendor-specific assumptions into the training pipeline; teacher sessions are logged with model/provider/version metadata and remain replaceable.

### AI 77. Opus teacher use

Anthropic Opus 5 is an approved teacher model for TemperTally under the written permission previously obtained.

The permission and its exact scope should be permanently archived with TemperTally training provenance.

Opus-class teachers are especially useful for:

- architecture;
- difficult coding;
- long-horizon tasks;
- critique;
- debugging;
- realistic agent trajectories.

---

### AI 78. Epistemic teacher use

Epistemics-focused open models such as Inkling are useful specifically for:

- calibration;
- confidence;
- “inspect first” examples;
- appropriate uncertainty;
- distinguishing answer/inspect/test/ask;
- long-context epistemic behavior.

TemperTally should learn the behavior without necessarily copying the teacher’s style.

### AI 79. Supervised teacher-student training

Teacher-based training should not be an opaque batch process.

The training framework should support **observable supervised teaching sessions** where the human can literally watch the larger model teach TemperTally.

A session may look conceptually like:

```text
Teacher:
presents task

Student:
attempts task

Teacher:
critiques

Student:
revises

Meridian verifier:
compiles / runs / tests / evaluates

Teacher:
reviews remaining failure

Student:
tries again

Verifier:
passes

Training system:
records successful trajectory
```

The teacher does not directly decide truth.

Meridian’s real execution environment remains the final authority whenever deterministic verification exists.

---

### AI 80. Human role in supervised teaching

“Supervised” does not mean manually clicking Approve on 200,000 samples.

The user should be able to:

- watch live teacher/student interaction;
- inspect any sample;
- pause;
- resume;
- reject a lesson;
- change the teacher;
- adjust curriculum;
- mark a teacher mistake;
- inspect verifier output;
- inspect current evaluation scores;
- inspect checkpoints;
- redirect training emphasis.

The workflow should allow unattended runs while preserving full observability and intervention.

### AI 82. Training resumability

Training must be aggressively restartable.

Persist:

```text

model state
```

### AI 83. TQF-based training framework

TurboQwenFare should eventually have a training subsystem sharing as much architecture as sensible with inference.

Conceptually:

```text
TurboQwenFare
├── inference
└── training
    ├── tensor store
    ├── tiered memory
    ├── expert residency
    ├── optimizer
    ├── gradient handling
    ├── activation handling
    ├── adapter training
    ├── selective expert training
    ├── distillation
    ├── RL
    ├── data streaming
    └── evaluation
```

After Meridian forks/integrates TQF, the Meridian-specific branch adds:

- Meridian-Gym;
- MeridianBench;
- teacher orchestration;
- Meridian curriculum;
- project/environment integrations;
- language-specific curricula;
- model-compression pipelines.

Prior planning already treated low-memory training, optimizer/gradient paging, recomputation, SSD/RAM streaming, and router-aware training as first-class TQF directions.

### AI 84. SSD-first low-memory training `AI-022`

> **Identifier provenance.** `AI-022` — *Consumer-hardware training stack*, locked in planning ledger v0.66 and restored here. The concept survived synthesis as AI 81–87; the stable identifier did not. The sequential `AI N.` numbering in this section is prose ordering and is **not** equivalent to the `AI-0NN` requirement family.

Training must treat storage as a tiered memory hierarchy:

```text
FAST / SMALL

GPU / unified memory
↓
system RAM
↓
fast NVMe SSD

SLOWER / HUGE
```

The framework should stream:

- cold experts;
- frozen weights;
- optimizer state;
- gradients where appropriate;
- activations;
- checkpoints;
- training shards.

The important question is not:

> “Can the entire 35B model fit in VRAM?”

It is:

> “What tensors does this operation need resident right now?”

---

### AI 85. SSD does not replace compute

The framework must acknowledge that NVMe solves capacity far more effectively than raw FLOP requirements.

Therefore most TemperTally development should avoid unnecessary full-parameter training.

Prefer:

- adapters;
- router training;
- expert-selective training;
- low-rank updates;
- compressed optimizer state;
- teacher-generated high-signal data;
- distillation;
- short targeted full-training stages only when justified.

The project should spend compute on **high-information training**, not brute-force token volume.

---

### AI 86. Multi-computer training

The framework should support using multiple personal machines where this is useful.

Do not assume consumer networking can substitute for NVLink-class synchronous model training.

Prefer embarrassingly parallel work such as:

- teacher generation;
- verification;
- benchmark runs;
- dataset preprocessing;
- independent candidate models;
- hyperparameter sweeps;
- pruning sweeps;
- simulation generation.

Core synchronous training may remain on one primary machine with SSD-backed state unless later networking research proves worthwhile.

---

### AI 87. Training stages

A proposed high-level curriculum:

#### Stage 0 — Baseline preservation

Benchmark the untouched base.

Establish:

- generic reasoning;
- coding;
- language ability;
- long-context performance;
- tool behavior.

#### Stage 1 — Meridian/domain continued training

Train on:

- Meridian source;
- engine architecture;
- graphics;
- physics;
- game development;
- compiler/runtime material;
- documentation.

#### Stage 2 — Multilingual specialization

Rust, Luau, C#, TypeScript, Python, Meridian Python, Anorak, shaders.

#### Stage 3 — Meridian tool/action SFT

Train actual Meridian APIs and editor operations.

#### Stage 4 — Epistemics

Train:

- inspect-first behavior;
- calibrated confidence;
- factual verification;
- false-premise rejection;
- appropriate questions;
- no-change decisions.

#### Stage 5 — Long context

Progressively extend real reasoning toward 1M.

#### Stage 6 — Meridian-Gym

Executable tasks with deterministic outcomes.

#### Stage 7 — Long-horizon agent RL

Whole-project creation, debugging, recovery, large refactors.

#### Stage 8 — UX/preference training

Normal human interaction, concise questions, corrections, low-friction collaboration.

#### Stage 9 — Compression

Pruning, slimming, expert merging, router recovery.

#### Stage 10 — Distillation

Frontier teachers + TemperTally Full → compressed students.

#### Stage 11 — Quantization recovery

Calibrate and recover Q5-ish shipping profile.

#### Stage 12 — release gating

Complete MeridianBench + safety + resource targets.

The older Meridian planning ledger already specified a multi-stage program including continued pretraining, multilingual/tool SFT, routing specialization, editor/vision training, Meridian Gym RL, long-horizon recovery training, preference training, quantization calibration, privacy testing, and MeridianBench gating.

### AI 90. Casual-user training

paired with the actual Meridian environment state needed to understand them.

The model should not require users to become prompt engineers.

### AI 91. Correction training

Train trajectories where the model misinterprets something and the human corrects it.

Correct behavior:

- update the task;
- stop invalid work;
- preserve useful evidence;
- avoid defensiveness;
- continue naturally.

Incorrect behavior:

- restart everything;
- repeat already answered questions;
- insist on the original interpretation;
- forget the correction later.

### AI 106. Development/dogfooding strategy

Before TemperTally is mature, build and harden the Meridian AI harness using large frontier models.

This allows the harness to become good **before** the local model is ready.

Development progression:

```text
Frontier models
    ↓
build/harden Meridian AI harness
    ↓
collect verified teaching tasks
    ↓
train TemperTally Full
    ↓
dogfood TemperTally Full
    ↓
Frontier models + TemperTally Full
    ↓
teach compressed TemperTally
```

Once TemperTally Full is good, use it heavily because:

- it knows Meridian natively;
- it has no per-token API cost;
- it can generate massive amounts of Meridian-specific data.

Still retain frontier models as independent teachers/critics.

TemperTally itself is intentionally **post-Meridian-1.0** and must not block the engine’s 1.0 release.

However, Meridian should become AI-ready before then through generally useful architecture.

Build:

Use frontier models.

#### Phase C — deep Meridian integration

Add:

- physics inspection;

- advanced debugger;
- profiler integration;
- incident history;
- experiments;
- extensions;
- verification.

#### Phase D — TQF integration

Integrate/fork mature TurboQwenFare.

Add:

- local inference;

- TQF index;

- expert streaming.

#### Phase E — training framework

Implement:

- SSD training;
- teachers;
- Training Observatory;
- Meridian-Gym;

#### Phase F — TemperTally Full

Train and specialize the full Qwen base.

#### Phase G — compression frontier

Expert profile/prune/slim/merge.

#### Phase H — distilled students

Train:

- ~12–16B sparse target;

Produce Meridian-specific Q5-ish model.

#### Phase J — release/dogfood

Release only after MeridianBench, safety, UX, context, and resource gates pass.

### AI 108. Hard requirements summary

The following should currently be treated as hard architectural/product constraints:

1. Meridian works entirely without AI.
2. AI installation is explicitly opt-in.
3. TemperTally is the official free local Meridian-specialized model.
4. TemperTally is not expected to universally beat frontier models.
5. Outside models receive rich Meridian access rather than artificial handicaps.
6. Third-party model usage is always visibly disclosed.
7. TemperTally requires at least 1,048,576 genuinely useful tokens of context.
8. The harness is deeply integrated with Meridian.
9. AI operates through real Meridian APIs.
10. The general Meridian APIs remain useful beyond AI.
11. The exact installed Meridian source is available for retrieval.
12. Questions are first-class.
13. A real read-only Planning mode exists.
14. Planning mode cannot mutate persistent project state.
15. The model cannot exit Planning mode itself.
16. TemperTally is trained to inspect before unsupported diagnosis.
17. TemperTally is trained to admit temporary uncertainty calmly.
18. The primary AI unit is a persistent task rather than only chat history.
19. Task constraints are structured and persistent.
20. Canonical task knowledge is not destroyed by context eviction.
21. 1M context is working memory rather than permanent storage.
22. Retrieval is repository/engine-aware rather than simple vector chunking.
23. Verification prefers deterministic execution over model confidence.
24. No-change is a valid successful outcome.
25. Runtime experiments are first-class.
26. Subagents are resource-aware and sparse by default.
27. Local subagents share one resident model rather than loading duplicate weights.
28. Subagents cannot gain capabilities their parent does not have.
29. Agents never use Git directly.
30. Source control goes through Meridian APIs.
31. External process execution is brokered.
32. Agents cannot perform irreversible destructive tasks.
33. There is no bypass-safety mode.
34. The Action Governor cannot be disabled by the agent.
35. Self-configuration cannot escalate authority.
36. Skills cannot expand authority.
37. `AGENTS.md` always exists at repository root.
38. Nested `AGENTS.md` exists only for genuinely scoped folder-specific rules.
39. `.meridian/` stores structured Meridian-specific state.
40. `AGENTS.md` is not replaced by `.meridian/`.
41. Meridian AI can safely configure its own operational settings.
42. Meridian AI can create and maintain skills.
43. Meridian AI can switch models according to user/provider policy.
44. Cost/privacy boundaries remain explicit.
45. Genuine Meridian limitations may be solved temporarily with proper Meridian extensions.
46. Temporary extensions are tracked for later migration/removal.
47. Meridian AI can fully prepare upstream bug/improvement issues.
48. GitHub issues can never be auto-published.
49. Human review and explicit human publication of GitHub issues are mandatory.
50. TemperTally should be deeply trained on Meridian source and implementation.
51. Rust, Luau, C#, TypeScript, Python, Meridian Python, Anorak and relevant shader languages receive explicit specialization.
52. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B is the current TemperTally Full starting point.
53. Expert pruning occurs only after routing/specialization profiling.
54. Fixed “one expert = one language” assignment is rejected.
55. TemperTally Full remains an internal teacher/reference.
56. A ~12–16B/~2B-active sparse descendant is a primary compression research target.
57. A 4–7B dense distilled model should also be investigated.
58. Main deployment quantization targets Q5-ish Meridian-aware mixed precision.
59. High-quality canonical training weights are preserved separately from deployment quantization.
60. TQF training must be designed for SSD-backed consumer-hardware operation.
61. Training must be highly resumable.
62. Multi-day local runs are an expected normal workflow.
63. Training must be thoroughly observable.
64. Frontier models perform much of the early teaching.
65. TemperTally Full later joins the teacher ensemble.
66. Teacher output is verified rather than trusted blindly.
67. Supervised teacher/student sessions are inspectable by the human.
68. Training-data contribution is opt-in.
69. Source-code contribution and AI-trajectory contribution are separate opt-ins.
70. MeridianBench compares TemperTally against frontier models honestly.
71. The AI UI should remain simple and non-cliché.
72. Most orchestration should be silent.
73. User attention should be treated as a limited resource.
74. The harness should optimize itself rather than exposing walls of performance knobs.
75. Meridian AI should make a normal developer more capable without requiring them to become an AI researcher.

### AI 110. Final design position

Meridian AI should not attempt to beat systems such as Claude Code by copying every feature those systems expose.

It should beat the experience by exploiting advantages those systems fundamentally do not have.

A terminal coding agent must reconstruct most of the world through:

- files;
- shell commands;
- logs;
- screenshots;
- user explanations.

Meridian AI can directly understand:

```text
what the user selected
what the user is looking at
what just happened
what changed
what source implemented it
what entity is involved
what physics event occurred
what render pass created a pixel
what resource consumed VRAM
what profiler span regressed
what test proves the fix
what project rule applies
what previous decision led here
```

Then combine that with:

```text
1M real context
+
first-party retrieval
+
Meridian source knowledge
+
typed APIs
+
real debugging
+
questions
+
persistent task state
+
deterministic verification
+
reversible transactions
+
safe self-configuration
+
resource-aware workers
+
frontier-model interoperability
+
TemperTally specialization
+
TQF low-memory execution
+
SSD-backed solo-developer training
```

The intended result is not:

> “A chatbot inside a game engine.”

It is:

> **A native intelligent development layer for Meridian that is powerful enough for experts, approachable enough for ordinary vibe-coded development, highly observable when desired, mostly invisible when it should be, and specifically engineered from the model weights through the engine APIs to make the AI unusually competent inside Meridian.**

TemperTally does not need to be the smartest model on Earth.

It needs to have the best possible home-field advantage.

And the entire Meridian AI architecture should be designed around giving it that advantage without ever preventing a larger outside model from taking full advantage of Meridian too.


### TurboQwenFare integrated runtime master contract `TQF-MASTER-001`

TurboQwenFare (TQF) is the Apache-2.0 model-specific inference/runtime technology used as the primary research and deployment foundation for TemperTally. The detailed TQF Master v2 contract below is integrated into this specoment so an implementation agent can build the runtime without consulting a separate document.

#### Reconciliation with current TemperTally direction

TQF Master v2 was written around a **Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4 standalone baseline**. That baseline remains valuable and concrete: it is the mandatory reference implementation used to prove the unusual out-of-core expert-streaming, memory-broker, context, retrieval, Metal and CUDA design.

Current Meridian AI direction adds these rules:

1. **Reference baseline vs final TemperTally profile.** Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4 is the TQF v1 reference/compatibility profile. TemperTally's expensive training base is revalidated immediately before training. If the winning base changes, TQF gains a new model-specific execution profile rather than pretending the old Qwen geometry is universal.
2. **Deployment precision.** The Q4 repack/reference path remains required for TQF correctness and the 4 GiB baseline. The main TemperTally deployment target is **Q5-ish Meridian-aware mixed precision**, selected by quality/resource evidence. TQF therefore must support model/profile-specific mixed precision without weakening the Q4 reference tests.
3. **Context.** The old `~1M` TQF target is sharpened for TemperTally to at least **1,048,576 genuinely useful tokens**, qualified for retrieval, coding, tool use, distractors and long-horizon tasks. A config limit alone is not success.
4. **Memory.** The **4 GiB default live working-set profile** remains an aggressive TQF acceptance target for the Qwen3.6 reference path; the 2 GiB profile remains experimental. A long-context/TemperTally profile may honestly require a larger budget where evidence shows it cannot satisfy quality and speed inside 4 GiB. The product reports the selected profile rather than lying about memory.
5. **Performance.** **>=15 decoded tok/s** remains the TQF qualification floor on the defined reference workloads/profiles, never the optimization stopping point. TTFT, prefill, stalls, tool turnaround and retrieval latency are co-equal product metrics.
6. **Reference hardware.** Base M4 MacBook Air 16 GiB remains the primary Apple reference. Linux + **RTX 3070 Ti** remains a mandatory NVIDIA reference, with >=6 GiB capable NVIDIA hardware as a target class. These are qualification profiles, not a rule that Meridian AI refuses to install anywhere else.
7. **Hardware eligibility UX.** Meridian/TQF uses capability-aware preflight and clearly distinguishes **Qualified**, **Best effort**, **Unsupported capability**, and **Insufficient resources**. It does not impose an arbitrary marketing hardware lock when the runtime can legally execute; neither does it advertise unqualified performance as Stable.
8. **One runtime, separate harness.** TQF remains an inference/runtime/server product, not the autonomous Meridian agent loop. The Meridian AI harness consumes it through typed provider/runtime interfaces.
9. **License.** TQF remains **Apache-2.0**. Model-weight licensing is handled separately; current TemperTally weight intent is Apache-2.0.
10. **Evidence wins.** Exact paging, cache, KV, sparse-attention, MTP, vector packing, ANN and I/O mechanisms remain benchmark-selected/research where Master v2 marks them as such. The first implementation that works does not become sacred.

The remainder of this TQF section is current implementation authority subject to those reconciliation rules.

#### TQF Decision-status vocabulary

Every nontrivial implementation statement in Master v2 belongs to one of four statuses. The status controls what an implementation agent may change without reopening product design.

| Status | Meaning | Change rule |
|---|---|---|
| **LOCKED** | Product/architecture contract already decided. | Do not change without an explicit architecture revision. |
| **REFERENCE BASELINE** | Concrete implementation required so correctness/performance can be measured. | Implement first; replace only after an A/B result proves a better path. |
| **RESEARCH CANDIDATE** | Deliberately experimental mechanism. | May fail; record the result in the optimization ledger. |
| **BENCHMARK-SELECTED** | Multiple valid implementations are specified. | The qualified benchmark winner becomes the machine/profile default. |

A phrase such as “benchmark this” is not permission to leave the subsystem unspecified. Master v2 always defines a reference baseline, the candidate variants, the metrics, and the selection/fallback rule.

**PART I**

**Mission, Product Contract, and Scope**

What TQF is, what it refuses to become, and the constraints every subsystem must respect.

#### TQF 1. Product thesis

TurboQwenFare is a local AI inference server specialized around Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4. Its external standard is Ollama-level simplicity; its internal standard is a hardware-aware research inference engine. The central bet is that sparse MoE activation, Qwen3.6’s hybrid recurrent/full-attention design, SSD streaming, model-specific kernels, aggressive memory virtualization, and continuous measurement can produce a user experience that conventional “load the model into RAM and run a generic graph” runtimes cannot.

The product must therefore optimize the entire path from model bytes on SSD to accepted output tokens: conversion layout, resident-core placement, expert cache admission, asynchronous reads, Metal/CUDA kernels, KV representation, long-context page selection, prefix reuse, request scheduling, and transient retrieval helpers. No single trick is expected to deliver the project goals. TQF is deliberately a system of coordinated optimizations.


> **The outside must remain boring.** A normal user should be able to run `tqf`, accept one model-download prompt, and receive a local server. The fact that the runtime may be moving expert tiles between SSD and unified memory, changing context precision, learning route statistics, and switching kernels under thermal pressure is implementation detail.


#### TQF 2. Non-goals and scope firewall

TurboQwenFare must not become a coding-agent harness merely because coding is an important benchmark and retrieval is useful. The runtime’s identity is “AI inference server.” Code-aware indexing is a retrieval capability; \`--open codex\` is compatibility glue. The model client remains responsible for editing files, running commands, applying patches, managing Git, and conducting agent loops.

- Not an IDE or editor.

- Not an autonomous agent loop.

- Not a shell/terminal orchestrator.

- Not a patch or Git-commit engine.

- Not a generic model-training or quantization toolkit.

- Not a generic tensor framework.

- Not a universal model runtime in v1.

- Not a vector-database product.

- Not a Python environment or plugin host.

This firewall should be reflected in source dependencies: core inference modules may not depend on retrieval, GUI, or client integration code. Optional layers consume the server/runtime; they do not infect it.

#### TQF 3. User-facing simplicity contract

**Intended normal command surface**


```text
tqf

tqf --headless

tqf --memory 8G

tqf --context 1M

tqf --enable-vision

tqf --host 0.0.0.0

tqf --model ./compatible-qwen36-q4.gguf

tqf sync .

tqf unsync .

tqf --open opencode

tqf --open claude

tqf --open codex

tqf status

tqf doctor

tqf optimize
```


Ordinary users must not have to understand GGUF variants, expert-cache slots, page-cache pressure, Metal command buffers, KV precision, embedding dimensions, ANN graph parameters, or MTP draft counts. Developer/debug controls may exist behind diagnostic commands or environment flags, but the product interface must prefer automatic policy.

#### TQF 4. Hard acceptance contract

| **Constraint**      | **Requirement** | **Interpretation**                                                             |
|---------------------|-----------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Model               | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | The production hot path may hard-code model shapes.                            |
| Weights             | Q4              | Initial conversion is lossless with respect to the source quantized values.    |
| Memory              | 4 GiB default   | Global live working-set budget, not “VRAM only.”                               |
| Experimental memory | 2 GiB           | A genuine hard wall; no hidden helper-model overflow.                          |
| Context             | 128K initial    | Logical context grows dynamically; no fixed 128K reservation on startup.       |
| Long context        | ~1M target      | 8 GiB may be required initially; API semantics remain stable.                  |
| Quality             | ≤1% degradation | Measured over coding, long-context, tool use, reasoning, and retrieval suites. |
| Speed               | ≥15 tok/s floor | Sustained decode floor; maximum attainable throughput remains the objective.   |
| Apple               | Base M4         | Primary implementation/reference backend.                                      |
| NVIDIA              | RTX 3070 Ti     | Mandatory Linux reference; ≥6 GiB capable NVIDIA GPUs are target class.        |
| Distribution        | One binary      | One Rust crate, no helper executables.                                         |

#### TQF 5. Performance philosophy

The project must not accidentally optimize for a benchmark that has unusually repetitive expert routing. NVMAI’s Qwen measurements demonstrate that decode rate can vary strongly by workload because expert-cache locality varies. Consequently, TQF’s headline numbers must include realistic coding and general workloads, and every performance report must show context length, memory budget, cache state, generation length, and hardware.

The optimization objective is user-perceived inference speed, not one scalar. Decode throughput matters, but time-to-first-token, prefill time, long-context stalls, tool-call turnaround, and retrieval latency also determine whether the server feels fast. A 28 tok/s configuration with 2-second TTFT can be preferable to a 31 tok/s configuration that stalls for 14 seconds before generation.

#### TQF 6. Quality philosophy

The ≤1% quality ceiling applies to the whole runtime stack. Exact weight-layout transformations should normally be bit/value preserving. Context quantization, sparse attention, retrieval-driven context building, MTP, and other approximate mechanisms must be qualified separately and in combination. The budget is not permission to spend 1% on every subsystem independently.

- Exact/lossless optimizations: prefer deterministic greedy-token parity and layerwise tensor checks.

- Numerically reordered but semantically exact kernels: use strict logit/intermediate tolerances.

- KV compression and sparse attention: measure long-context retrieval, coding, reasoning, perplexity/logit drift, and tool behavior.

- Retrieval: evaluate recall, ranking, downstream task success, and hallucination/false-context failure modes.

- Vision: qualify multimodal behavior separately because text-only mode intentionally keeps vision unloaded.

**PART II**

**Qwen3.6 Anatomy and Feasibility Mathematics**

Exact architecture facts, derived tensor sizes, and why this particular MoE model is suited to out-of-core inference.

#### TQF 7. Why Qwen3.6-35B-A3B

Qwen’s official model card describes Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as a 35B-total, 3B-activated causal language model with a vision encoder. The language model uses 40 layers in a repeating 3:1 pattern: three Gated DeltaNet + MoE layers followed by one gated full-attention + MoE layer, repeated ten times. It has hidden size 2048, 256 routed experts, top-8 routing plus one shared expert, expert intermediate width 512, and native context 262,144 with documented extension to roughly 1,010,000 tokens. \[R1\]\[R2\]

This combination is unusually favorable to TQF. Sparse routed experts make the majority of MoE parameters streamable instead of continuously resident. Only ten layers require conventional growing K/V history. The other thirty layers use recurrent Gated DeltaNet state whose main state size is independent of context length. Qwen also ships an MTP component and can be served text-only without loading the vision encoder, directly supporting TQF’s lazy-vision design. \[R1\]

#### TQF 8. Canonical language architecture

| **Property**         | **Value**                   | **Why it matters**                                                              |
|----------------------|-----------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Total parameters     | 35B                         | Large enough to be genuinely capable; too large for naive low-memory residency. |
| Activated parameters | ~3B/token                   | Sparse compute enables out-of-core expert streaming.                            |
| Hidden size          | 2048                        | Allows highly specialized fixed-shape kernels.                                  |
| Layers               | 40                          | Scheduling loop is fixed and hard-codeable.                                     |
| Layer pattern        | 30 GDN + 10 full attention  | Long-context KV grows in only 25% of layers.                                    |
| GDN heads            | 32 V / 16 QK, dim 128       | Recurrent state is predictable and constant-size with context.                  |
| Full attention       | 16 Q / 2 KV, dim 256        | Low KV-head count makes long context much cheaper than classic MHA.             |
| RoPE dim             | 64                          | Only a sub-dimension is rotary, opening pre-RoPE/compressed-key opportunities.  |
| Experts              | 256/layer                   | Large cold expert pool; strong need for cache policy.                           |
| Top-K                | 8 routed + 1 shared         | 320 routed expert selections per decoded token across 40 layers.                |
| Expert width         | 512                         | Each routed expert is relatively small and tileable.                            |
| Vocab                | 248,320                     | Large output head is a bandwidth-sensitive hot tensor.                          |
| MTP                  | 1 hidden layer in config    | Useful only if accepted-token throughput wins in real tests.                    |
| GDN state dtype      | float32 in reference config | Recurrent-state fidelity must be handled carefully.                             |

#### TQF 9. Exact routed-expert weight math

The Transformers implementation represents each routed expert with gate, up, and down projections. With D=2048 and expert intermediate F=512, one expert contains 2048×512 gate weights, 2048×512 up weights, and 512×2048 down weights: 3,145,728 weights total. \[R3\]

**Derived expert-size calculation**


```text
expert_weights = 3 × 2048 × 512
               = 3,145,728 weights
raw_Q4_payload = 3,145,728 × 4 / 8
               = 1,572,864 bytes
               = 1.500 MiB per expert (before Q4 metadata)
```


A token selects 8 routed experts in each of 40 layers, or 320 routed-expert selections. If every selection missed and the on-disk Q4 layout were an ideal raw four bits/weight, routed payload would be 480 MiB/token. NVMAI’s Q4 slot accounting is around 1.55 MiB/expert in its format, implying about 496 MiB/token under 100% miss behavior. That translates to roughly 7.27 GiB/s of expert bytes at 15 tok/s, 9.69 GiB/s at 20 tok/s, and 14.53 GiB/s at 30 tok/s. \[R8–R11\]


> **Interpretation:** The bandwidth calculation is an upper-bound planning model, not a claim that TQF will read that many bytes. Expert hits, partial residency, coalesced reads, predictor overlap, shared-expert compute, OS/storage caching, and MTP can all reduce effective bytes per accepted output token. The optimization target should explicitly track SSD bytes/accepted token.


#### TQF 10. Full-attention KV math

Only ten language layers use conventional full attention. Each has two KV heads of dimension 256. For both K and V, BF16 storage therefore requires 10 × 2 × 2 × 256 × 2 bytes = 20 KiB per context token. This is the central long-context capacity calculation.

| **Logical context** | **BF16 KV payload** | **Approx. raw Q4 payload** | **Planning implication**                                               |
|---------------------|---------------------|----------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 4K                  | 0.078 GiB           | ~0.020 GiB                 | Easy.                                                                  |
| 8K                  | 0.156 GiB           | ~0.039 GiB                 | Easy; large expert cache remains.                                      |
| 32K                 | 0.625 GiB           | ~0.156 GiB                 | Still comfortable in 4G.                                               |
| 128K                | 2.50 GiB            | ~0.625 GiB                 | Compression is mandatory for a useful expert cache.                    |
| 256K                | 5.00 GiB            | ~1.25 GiB                  | Low-bit TQKV required in 4G.                                           |
| 1.01M               | ~19.26 GiB          | ~4.82 GiB                  | Compression alone may fit 8G, but attention bandwidth requires TQAttn. |

Raw Q4 is not the final TQKV size because scales, outlier metadata, search signatures, page metadata, and mixed-precision policies add overhead. Conversely, TQKV is allowed to use 2–3-bit cold pages, random rotations, pre-RoPE storage, and richer SSD backing, so the average in-memory bit rate may be lower than four bits while staying inside the ≤1% quality limit.

#### TQF 11. Gated DeltaNet state math

The reference recurrent implementation repeats Q/K from 16 key heads to 32 value heads and maintains a state shaped approximately \[32, 128, 128\] in float32 for each GDN layer. That is about 2 MiB per GDN layer, or roughly 60 MiB across 30 layers, plus a relatively small convolution tail. This state is constant-size with context length. \[R2\]\[R3\]

This is one of the most important structural reasons TQF can pursue huge logical context. A classic 40-layer Transformer would grow KV in all 40 layers; Qwen3.6 grows conventional KV in ten. The recurrent state still requires precision, snapshotting, and efficient updates, but it does not scale from hundreds of megabytes to tens of gigabytes as the prompt grows.

#### TQF 12. Other high-value tensors

The 248,320×2048 token embedding table and untied output head are each approximately 508.6M weights. At raw four-bit payload they are each roughly 242.5 MiB before quantization metadata. Their runtime behavior differs: only the current input-token row needs to be gathered from the embedding table during decode, while the entire output head participates in next-token logits. Therefore the embedding table is a strong candidate for nonresident/random-row access, while the LM head is a high-value hot tensor and kernel-optimization target.

The dense GDN projection weights, ten full-attention blocks, shared experts, routers, norms, and output head collectively form the always-used core. Exact converted tensor accounting must replace rough planning estimates before the memory broker is finalized. TQF must ship a developer command that prints exact resident candidates by tensor, bytes, quant type, and access frequency.

#### TQF 13. Canonical checkpoint set

The current ggml-org Qwen3.6 GGUF repository exposes a Q4_K_M language checkpoint of 20.4 GB, a Q4_0 MTP artifact of 1.06 GB, and a Q8_0 vision projector of 614 MB. The Q4_K_M file publishes SHA-256 671e47e0ec53c665d048b98c3ecbfd5236b5ca9c3e02ed19fc8f81f7b85140c7. TQF should pin an immutable source revision rather than following a moving “main.” \[R4\]


> **Pinned-source rule:** The exact source commit/hash used by a TQF release is part of the release contract. `tqf update` may offer a newly qualified model revision; startup must never silently swap model bytes under an existing benchmark/correctness profile.


**PART III**

**Research Landscape and Prior Art**

What has already been proven, what has failed, what is worth stealing under Apache-2.0, and where TQF must invent new work.

#### TQF 14. TurboFieldfare: foundational systems precedent

TurboFieldfare demonstrates the core out-of-core MoE idea on Apple Silicon: keep a shared/resident core in memory, stream only selected routed experts from SSD, maintain a bounded expert cache, overlap shared-expert compute with expert reads, and perform bounded-memory model installation by repacking remote byte ranges directly rather than staging an entire source checkpoint. Its public measurements span an 8 GB M2 Air at roughly 5.1–6.3 tok/s and a 24 GB M5 Pro at roughly 31–35 tok/s for its Gemma 4 target. \[R7\]

TQF should treat TurboFieldfare as permanent upstream research input. The specific model differs, but the system principles—bounded memory, explicit expert streaming, measurement-driven kernel work, and a model-specific format—are directly aligned. Because TurboFieldfare is Apache-2.0, implementation may be adapted with correct attribution rather than re-created from memory.

#### TQF 15. NVMAI: direct Qwen3.6 donor and negative-results database

NVMAI is a focused Apache-2.0 fork of TurboFieldfare for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. It is particularly valuable because it has already implemented the hybrid Qwen graph, Gated DeltaNet, Q4/6/8-bit paths, model repacking, server support, and extensive optimization instrumentation. TQF should mine both code and experiment history, while replacing architectural choices that conflict with the global 4 GiB budget. \[R8\]

| **NVMAI finding**             | **Measured effect / conclusion**                                               | **TQF action**                                                                       |
|-------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Parallel expert pread         | Q4 M3 I/O wall about 41.2→30.9 ms/token; decode 9.98→12.80 tok/s (+28%).       | Port concept immediately; autotune worker count. \[R9\]                              |
| 64 cache slots + resident pin | ~10% decode gain vs 32+pin; 128 slots could regress from pressure.             | Keep pinning lesson, replace fixed per-layer cache with global broker. \[R10\]       |
| MoE phase-1 MSL rewrite       | Stage 14.4→9.24 ms/token; byte-identical deterministic output.                 | Adapt kernel, then specialize harder for M4/Q4. \[R11\]                              |
| 4096-token prefill chunk      | 1280-token prompt ~13.6s vs 43.3s for 128-token chunks; ~13% faster than 1024. | Start autotune around large MoE-aware chunks. \[R12\]                                |
| Fused GDN input projections   | Four Q4 GEMVs fused; stage reduction measured, exact math preserved.           | Adapt and extend fusion. \[R13\]                                                     |
| Targeted F_RDADVISE           | ~10.6% gain in one M3 Q4 test; neutral elsewhere.                              | Autotune per host; never universalize. \[R16\]                                       |
| Persistent KV + GDN snapshots | Demonstrates hybrid-state prefix restore.                                      | Replace monolithic snapshot payloads with deduplicated TQKV page references. \[R14\] |
| CPU MTP drafting              | Output-head bandwidth erased hoped-for CPU advantage.                          | Do not prioritize CPU draft path; keep GPU MTP benchmark-driven. \[R15\]             |
| Stage accounting              | Corrected GPU budget exposed attention and routed MoE as major costs.          | Build detailed timing from day one. \[R8\]                                           |

#### TQF 16. What TQF must not copy from NVMAI

NVMAI’s larger expert-cache configurations allocate slots per layer and can consume several gigabytes just for routed expert cache. That design is reasonable on a 24 GB host but conflicts with TQF’s rule that the whole active system should fit in 4 GiB by default. TQF therefore takes the measured lesson—expert residency is enormously valuable—but implements a global byte-budgeted cache that can move capacity toward layers and expert tiles with the highest marginal value.

- Do not inherit a multi-target Swift package architecture; TQF remains one Rust crate/one binary.

- Do not inherit fixed equal per-layer cache budgets.

- Do not inherit text-only scope; TQF supports lazy vision behind \`--enable-vision\`.

- Do not assume MTP is beneficial merely because the model was trained for it.

- Do not expose a wall of expert/cache knobs to normal users; autotune and self-tune instead.

- Do not treat 256K as the final context target; TQF explicitly pursues ~1M.

#### TQF 17. MoE caching/offload research

FlashMoE is directly relevant because it treats SSD I/O, not arithmetic, as the key bottleneck in memory-constrained MoE inference. Its paper reports a lightweight ML-based cache policy that combines reuse signals and can improve cache hit rate by up to 51% over LRU/LFU in its evaluated setups, with up to 2.6× system speedup. TQF should use this as evidence that a learned/adaptive admission policy is worth benchmarking, not as permission to copy results to Qwen. \[R23\]

MoEpic provides complementary evidence for partial-expert residency: split experts into segments, cache hot portions, predict next-layer use, and allocate per-layer cache budget adaptively. Its evaluated systems report sizable latency reductions versus its baselines. TQF’s tiled \`.tqf\` format is intentionally designed so the runtime can investigate this class of partial-expert strategy without a format rewrite. \[R24\]

#### TQF 18. Long-context KV compression research

TurboQuant is especially aligned with TQF because it treats high-dimensional vectors geometrically rather than as arbitrary scalar blocks. It uses random rotation plus quantization and provides an inner-product-oriented formulation. The paper reports quality neutrality around 3.5 bits/channel and only marginal degradation around 2.5 bits/channel in its evaluated KV-cache tasks. This motivates TQKV’s research into rotated, low-bit, inner-product-preserving key representations. \[R18\]

KVQuant and KIVI show that Keys and Values should not automatically use identical quantization rules. KVQuant emphasizes per-channel Keys, pre-RoPE Key quantization, non-uniform datatypes, and explicit outlier handling; KIVI similarly finds per-channel Keys and per-token Values effective at two bits in its tested models. These techniques are starting hypotheses. Qwen3.6-specific sensitivity must be re-measured because it uses only ten full-attention layers, GQA, partial rotary dimensions, and a different model distribution. \[R19\]\[R20\]

#### TQF 19. Long-context sparse attention research

Quest establishes the useful separation between retaining a KV cache and reading every KV page for every query. It scores pages from Key statistics and the current Query, then loads only the most critical pages. This is conceptually close to TQAttn: preserve logical context, always include recent/protected content, and reduce memory movement rather than permanently deleting history. \[R21\]

Self-Indexing KVCache pushes the idea further by designing compressed Key representations that also act as the sparse-attention index. TQF should explicitly investigate whether TQKV Key pages can provide cheap search signatures so a separate million-token ANN structure is unnecessary. \[R22\]

#### TQF 20. Vector-index research for TQIndex

Quake and SPFresh are relevant not because TQF should clone either system, but because they demonstrate two requirements of a live code/document index: partitions should adapt to skewed query/update workloads, and local edits should trigger local repair rather than periodic global rebuilds. Quake uses workload-adaptive hierarchical partitioning and dynamic query parameters; SPFresh uses localized in-place partition repair. TQIndex should combine those principles with something generic ANN systems do not possess: repository hierarchy and exact program structure. \[R25\]\[R26\]

CoIR and RepoBench provide external evaluation baselines for code retrieval and repository-scale code completion/retrieval. TQIndex should also add project-specific tests over real repositories because generic benchmark recall does not reveal whether the retriever found the exact implementation, caller, test, configuration, or recent diff an agent actually needed. \[R27\]\[R28\]

#### TQF 21. Hardware I/O research

Apple Metal exposes I/O command queues capable of loading file data into Metal resources and synchronizing I/O with GPU work. TQF should benchmark Metal I/O against explicit parallel \`pread\`, read-ahead, and shared-buffer paths on the base M4 rather than assuming the newer API wins. \[R29\]

On NVIDIA, GPUDirect Storage provides an explicit direct DMA path between storage and GPU memory on supported systems, but NVIDIA’s current design guidance lists Quadro/Data Center class GDS-capable GPUs, not consumer GeForce as the baseline. The RTX 3070 Ti path therefore must be designed around explicit asynchronous SSD reads into pinned host staging plus \`cudaMemcpyAsync\`; GDS is an optional fast path on qualifying machines. \[R30\]

**PART IV**

**Top-Level Runtime Architecture and Source Organization**

One crate, one binary, strict dependency direction, explicit execution ownership, and a scheduler that understands Qwen rather than generic graph nodes.

#### TQF 22. System decomposition

**Logical architecture**


```text
CLIENTS

OpenAI / Anthropic / Ollama / GUI / MCP / integrations

│

▼

Request Normalizer

│

optional TQIndex RAG

│

▼

Session Scheduler

│

▼

Qwen3.6 Execution Core

┌──────────────┼──────────────┐

▼ ▼ ▼

TQKV/TQAttn Expert Runtime Prefix Runtime

└──────────────┼──────────────┘

▼

Memory Broker

┌───────────┼───────────┐

▼ ▼ ▼

Metal/CUDA CPU SIMD SSD
```


The core runtime owns Qwen execution and memory. Server code normalizes protocols into one internal request representation. Retrieval may augment an input, but the model core remains valid with retrieval entirely disabled. The GUI talks to local server/control endpoints rather than maintaining a second inference implementation in Swift.

#### TQF 23. One-crate source tree

The project is intentionally not split into a Cargo workspace. Logical boundaries live as Rust modules and folders inside one crate. This avoids internal package-management overhead while still allowing clear unsafe/FFI boundaries, feature-gated platform code, and unit testing.

**Normative module layout**


```text
src/

main.rs

build.rs

app/

cli/

config/

setup/

format/{tqf,gguf,quant}/

model/qwen36/

runtime/

memory/

experts/

context/{tqkv,tqattn,prefix}/

io/

backend/{metal,cuda}/

simd/

tokenizer/

sampling/

vision/

server/{openai,anthropic,ollama,tqf_api}/

retrieval/

mcp/

integrations/

gui/macos/

metrics/

bench/

dev/
```


#### TQF 24. Dependency firewall

| **From**      | **May depend on**                                  | **Must not depend on**       |
|---------------|----------------------------------------------------|------------------------------|
| model/runtime | memory, backend, IO, tokenizer, sampling           | retrieval, GUI, integrations |
| server        | runtime, retrieval facade, protocols               | GUI                          |
| retrieval     | memory broker, helper-model runtime, parsers, SIMD | GUI, coding-client internals |
| GUI           | local control/server interfaces                    | model internals              |
| integrations  | server/MCP launch/config helpers                   | model kernels                |
| backend       | platform FFI, shared tensor metadata               | retrieval/product logic      |

#### TQF 25. Async and thread model

Tokio should handle non-differentiating asynchronous control work: HTTP, SSE transport, downloads, filesystem watching, MCP, process integration, and background maintenance. The token-critical inference loop must use dedicated threads/queues and explicit GPU/I/O synchronization. The goal is deterministic control over when router results become visible to the CPU, when expert reads begin, which buffers they fill, and which command buffer consumes them.

The runtime should maintain a single active decode request in v1 and queue others, with clean cancellation. Later continuous batching may share the loaded model across sessions, but batch-1 latency/throughput remains the core performance objective and must not regress silently.

#### TQF 26. Internal request/session model

**Illustrative internal API (not final Rust syntax)**


```text
struct NormalizedRequest {

protocol: ProtocolFlavor,

messages: Vec<Message>,

tools: Vec<ToolDefinition>,

sampling: SamplingParams,

logical_context_limit: usize,

retrieval: RetrievalPolicy,

vision: Vec<VisionInput>,

stream: bool,

}

struct Session {

id: SessionId,

token_history: TokenStore,

context: ContextState,

prefix: Option<PrefixHandle>,

cancellation: CancellationToken,

}
```


Protocol-specific semantics are normalized at the boundary. OpenAI Responses events, Chat Completions chunks, Anthropic Messages events, and Ollama streams should all consume one generation event stream internally. This avoids protocol handling inside the model loop.

#### TQF 27. Unsafe policy

Early research may use \`unsafe\` aggressively in the places that genuinely need it: Metal/CUDA FFI, aligned/mapped storage, SIMD, zero-copy buffer wrapping, Swift bridging, and direct I/O. As paths stabilize, the project should move unsafety behind small audited modules and safe ownership APIs. The objective is not a cosmetically low unsafe-line count; it is a comprehensible safety boundary without sacrificing performance.

**PART V**

**Model Acquisition, Conversion, and the .tqf Container**

How a user gets from one binary to a verified hardware-optimized Qwen installation without knowing anything about model formats.

#### TQF 28. First-run state machine

**First-run lifecycle**


```text
START

│

├─ detect OS / CPU / GPU / memory / storage

├─ load global config and hardware profile

├─ validate trusted model receipt

│ └─ missing/invalid → model setup

│

├─ model setup asks: Download and optimize? [Y/n]

│ ├─ n → exit

│ └─ y → resolve pinned source → download/range-read → verify → repack → finalize

│

├─ short hardware autotune

├─ start server

└─ on macOS desktop, launch SwiftUI unless --headless
```


The setup process must be transactional. An interrupted network transfer or conversion leaves a resumable partial installation, never a model directory that appears valid. The final \`.tqf\` becomes visible to the runtime only after all required extents, metadata, and checksums validate and the final atomic rename/receipt write succeeds.

#### TQF 29. Source resolution and pinning

A release embeds exact expected source IDs and hashes. The canonical path is a pinned Q4 language checkpoint plus matching MTP data; vision is lazy/optional. Experimental \`--model\` imports may accept compatible Qwen3.6 Q4 files, but they do not inherit the canonical performance guarantee until separately qualified.

If TQF itself downloads a temporary source artifact solely for conversion, it may delete that temporary source after successful verified conversion. If the user pointed TQF at an existing file or an Ollama-owned blob, TQF must not delete the source. Ownership is explicit, not inferred from filename.

#### TQF 30. Streaming remote repack

The ideal installer never materializes a complete source GGUF and complete target \`.tqf\` simultaneously.
