Later research may add per-finger collision, richer surface wrapping, physical finger constraints, grip-force estimation, high-fidelity VR hands, and physical climbing fingers without changing the public high-level grip contract.

#### Validation

Qualification includes objects across diameter/shape ranges, different hand proportions, mirrored rigs, two-handed objects, moving objects, climbing/support contacts, low-LOD transitions, and failure cases where geometry cannot satisfy the requested grip.

### Layered production facial-performance stack `ARTUS-009` — *Normative*

Artus 1.0 includes a real facial-performance system rather than postponing all meaningful facial animation until after 1.0.

#### Semantic facial profile

A facial profile maps semantic controls—jaw, lips, smile/frown, brow, cheek, blink/squint, eye direction, and other supported controls—to the target character's actual blendshapes, bones, procedural transforms, or stylized substitutes. The mapping must support blendshape-only, bone-driven, hybrid, stylized, and eye-only rigs.

#### Layering

The runtime composes base expression, emotional/style state, speech/visemes, gaze/eyes, blink, gameplay reactions, breathing/subtle motion, and authored overrides with explicit priorities and masks. The exact semantic control vocabulary remains open until the facial-standard round, but the layered contract is locked.

#### Speech and Wavefront boundary

Wavefront owns audio playback and timing. Artus owns visual facial performance. Meridian may provide deterministic or signal-analysis tools that create editable phoneme/viseme starting alignments from dialogue audio, but generated alignment is never treated as untouchable authority. Dialogue waveforms, caption/word timing, phonemes/visemes, expressions, eye cues, and overrides should be co-editable in the performance tooling.

#### Gaze coordination

Eye, head, neck, and torso gaze behavior must be coordinated through Artus rather than independent look-at systems that fight each other. Gaze weighting and timing should depend on target angle, urgency, style, physical limits, and current interaction.

#### Graceful capability degradation

Characters without facial rigs continue to use body animation normally. Eye-only rigs can still support gaze/blink. LOD may reduce the facial stack from full solve to simplified speech/blink, static expression, or no evaluation.

#### Validation

Qualification includes differing facial rig technologies, dialogue sync, gaze transitions, authored overrides, body/face handoff in Sequencer, LOD transitions, and characters with partial/no facial capability.

### Automatic multi-tier character-motion representation `ARTUS-010` — *Normative*

Artus LOD is a representation system coordinated by Meridian's performance governor, not only distance thresholds that toggle a few animation features.

#### Importance inputs

Character motion importance may consider visibility, screen size, camera distance, player ownership, gameplay importance, interaction state, cinematic status, network authority, physical relevance, current performance budgets, and project pins/overrides.

#### Representation tiers

Qualified implementations may include hero, near, mid, far, and non-articulated aggregate/off-screen tiers. Higher tiers can use full skeletons, motion matching, full-body IK, physical animation, hands, face, and all important contacts. Lower tiers may use reduced skeletons, lower update frequencies, interpolation, reduced motion-search features, fewer IK/contact solves, simplified gaze/face, or no articulated pose evaluation when the character is off-screen and only simulation semantics matter.

#### Promotion/demotion continuity

Representation changes must preserve enough semantic state—locomotion state, gait, phase, root trajectory, style, important contacts, and interaction state—to reconstruct a coherent higher-detail pose without obvious state resets. Promotion/demotion is hysteretic and traceable.

#### Gameplay exception

Visual distance alone cannot force a low semantic/physical tier when the character remains gameplay-critical. A distant network player, sniper, boss, or physics-critical carrier may retain higher authoritative state with a cheaper visual representation.

#### Disabled cost and headless products

Headless servers may run compact Artus semantic/network state with no deformation or presentation-only pose work. Fine presentation tiers must not leak into dedicated-server packages when unused.

#### Validation

Benchmarks cover one hero, groups of detailed characters, hundreds/thousands of lower-detail characters, repeated LOD crossings, networked characters, web profiles, and budget pressure. The profiler must explain why a character occupies its current tier and estimated savings/cost.

### Semantic Artus networking with authority tiers `ARTUS-011` — *Normative*

Artus networking defaults to compact semantic replication rather than continuous replication of every bone transform.

#### Replicated state

Depending on topology/profile, replication may include authoritative root state, Motion Intent/state identifiers, trajectory or locomotion state, important Motion Source identifiers/phases, gameplay-critical contacts, Smart Interaction state, physical-animation authority state, ragdoll state, and bounded corrections.

#### Authority classes

Artus state is classified as: (1) gameplay-authoritative state, such as root position, support contacts, gameplay-relevant grabs, ragdoll collision state, and interaction completion; (2) reconstructable presentation state, such as locomotion/motion-source phase when needed for coherent synthesis; and (3) pure presentation state, such as minor finger fitting, blink noise, breathing, or cosmetic IK.

Clients synthesize detailed pose, IK, gaze, fingers, facial micro-motion, and other noncritical presentation locally when the network profile allows it. Gameplay correctness must never depend on clients independently choosing the same cosmetic pose.

#### Reconciliation and rollback

Corrections should use root reconciliation, pose inertialization, contact-aware correction, and intent/state replay rather than teleporting bones. Rollback-capable profiles distinguish rewindable simulation-relevant Artus state from presentation-only state. Host migration snapshots include the compact authoritative/migratable Artus state rather than opaque runtime pointers.

#### Validation

Qualification includes latency, jitter, loss, host migration, late join, LOD differences between peers, rollback profiles, ragdoll/contact transitions, and malicious/invalid state. Bandwidth and correction magnitude must be measured rather than inferred.

### Error-bounded semantics-aware animation compilation and compression `ARTUS-012` — *Normative*

Animation source data compiles into target- and quality-specific runtime products under explicit error budgets. No single codec or third-party library is locked by this decision.

#### Semantic error budgets

The compiler can reason separately about translation, rotation, scale, morph/facial curves, root motion, end-effector error, contact timing, and motion-matching features. Contact-critical feet/hands, root trajectories, and close-up facial controls may receive stricter bounds than unconstrained joints.

#### Derived products

One authoritative source animation may produce hero/native, NPC, crowd, web, cinematic, and motion-search products without duplicating the source asset. Motion-search features and pose/clip payloads are separate residency products so search does not require all full-precision animation data resident.

#### Streaming/runtime

Long clips and performances may use compressed streaming/decompression windows, SIMD-friendly packed representations, pose caches, and skeleton-specific mappings. The asset compiler owns deterministic cooking, target specialization, versioning, and provenance.

#### Research policy

Meridian should benchmark permissively licensed compression libraries/algorithms and independent implementations. Direct adaptation follows the permissive-only mining/provenance policy. The final codec choice requires measured quality, decode cost, memory, build time, streaming behavior, web portability, and maintenance evidence.

#### Validation

Automated tests compare root trajectory, contact timing, end-effector deviation, joint angular error, facial-curve error, decompression cost, memory, seek/stream behavior, and cross-platform determinism where required.

### CPU-authoritative hybrid CPU/GPU Artus execution `ARTUS-013` — *Normative*

Artus is designed for heterogeneous execution, but gameplay-critical semantics must remain available without requiring GPU readback or even graphics hardware.

#### Execution classes

Compiled Artus work may execute on simulation CPU, worker CPU, SIMD batches, qualified GPU compute, or Penumbra deformation paths. Developers declare semantic requirements and budgets; Meridian's scheduler/performance governor chooses execution placement.

#### CPU authority

Root motion, Motion Intents, gameplay-critical contacts, Smart Interaction state, physical-animation state, authoritative pose queries, networking state, and other gameplay-facing semantics maintain a CPU-available authoritative representation. Dedicated/headless servers remain fully functional without a GPU.

#### GPU candidates

Qualified GPU work may include large-crowd clip sampling, pose blending, skeleton-matrix generation, deformation/skinning, blendshape evaluation, selected procedural layers, and measured motion-search work. These are optimization products rather than the only source of character truth.

#### Penumbra boundary

Artus owns motion meaning, semantic joints, source selection, and animation state. Penumbra owns rendering/deformation scheduling and GPU render resources. Shared compiled deformation products may cross the boundary without making Penumbra the character-animation authority.

#### Readback prohibition

The default architecture must not require synchronous GPU-to-CPU readback because gameplay asks for a hand, contact, or root position. Such semantic data is maintained on CPU or consumed through explicitly latency-tolerant snapshots.

#### Recovery and web

GPU-resident animation/deformation caches are derived state and recoverable after device loss. WebGPU paths may offload qualified work, but reduced/single-thread/browser profiles retain correct gameplay semantics with alternate execution.

### Full Artus motion causality, timeline, and explanation suite `ARTUS-014` — *Normative*

Artus automation requires unusually strong observability. The editor must provide more than graph-state inspection and skeleton overlays.

#### Motion Trace

Development builds can record a bounded semantic Motion Trace containing intents, desired/achieved trajectories, source selections, motion-matching candidate choices/costs, contacts, IK constraint results, Cairn disagreement, physical-authority changes, network corrections, LOD transitions, facial/gaze events, and timing/cost attribution.

#### Timeline

The Artus debugger aligns intent, trajectory, Motion Source, graph/motion-search state, contacts, IK/constraint error, Cairn movement, physical authority, networking, LOD, facial/gaze state, and frame cost on a scrub-able timeline. Raw evidence must remain available under higher-level explanations.

#### Explainability

The system should answer questions such as why a foot slid, why a character stopped, why a particular motion candidate won, why a hand contact released, why an interaction failed, why a network correction changed the pose, why a feature disappeared at an LOD, and why Artus exceeded a frame budget. Explanations cite the responsible source asset/profile, constraint/contact, subsystem result, and timing interval.

#### Comparison tooling

Synchronized comparisons should support profile before/after, different target rigs, motion databases, native/web products, local/networked execution, LOD tiers, and CPU/GPU execution where meaningful. Quantitative trajectory/contact/error/cost overlays accompany visual comparison.

#### Automated torture stages

In addition to flat ground, slopes, stairs, rubble, moving platforms, doors, chairs, ladders, obstacles, impacts, and ragdolls, Artus qualification includes arbitrary gravity, zero-G contacts, latency/loss, extreme proportions, low frame rates, missing motion-database coverage, LOD transitions, and CPU/GPU placement changes.

#### Shipping diagnostics

Projects may retain a bounded, low-cost semantic trace ring in qualified shipping builds for bug reports without continuously recording every bone transform. Disabled shipping trace support must have documented/verified cost.

### Artus unresolved implementation work — *Open implementation research*

The locked decisions above intentionally do not choose: exact finger solver; exact semantic facial control standard; speech/phoneme-analysis method; crowd tier thresholds; network packet encoding/compression; rollback storage representation; animation compression codec; GPU kernel architecture; deformation IR; or exact trace serialization. Those require dedicated research/prototype decisions.

---


## Detailed navigation contract


### Multiple first-party navigation representations under common semantics `NAV-001` — *Normative*

Meridian navigation is not architecturally limited to one navmesh representation. NAV supports multiple representation families where their domain benefits justify them, while exposing a coherent set of agent, traversal, query, cost, link, and diagnostic concepts.

#### User-visible contract

A developer should normally think in terms of:

- where an agent may move;
- what movement capabilities it has;
- what a route costs;
- what dynamic conditions currently block or alter traversal;
- whether a destination is reachable;
- which representation NAV chose and why.

They should not need to select a particular spatial data structure merely to make an ordinary walking NPC navigate a level.

#### Representation families

The complete architecture may support, independently or in combination:

- **surface navigation meshes** for continuous walkable surfaces;
- **graphs/portals/waypoint structures** for coarse routing, authored topology, special traversal, or highly structured environments;
- **grids and cost fields** for tactical fields, dense regularly sampled spaces, flow computation, or specialized simulation;
- **flow-field products** for large groups sharing destinations or strategic gradients;
- **volumetric navigation** for swimming, flight, zero-G, free-space movement, or other 3D traversal volumes;
- **oriented-surface navigation** for walls, ceilings, arbitrary-gravity surfaces, planetary/local gravity frames, and non-world-up traversal;
- **dedicated 2D navigation products** appropriate to Meridian's first-class 2D runtime rather than a hidden flattened 3D implementation;
- **specialized domain products** for vehicles, rails, lanes, ladders, climbing surfaces, jump links, portals, elevators, doors, moving platforms, and similar traversal semantics.

This is a portfolio under one NAV contract, not a requirement to instantiate every representation in every project or region.

#### Common semantic layer

Representations share concepts such as:

- stable navigation region identity;
- traversal links and transitions;
- agent capability profiles;
- cost classes and dynamic cost modifiers;
- path/query snapshots;
- source-to-runtime provenance;
- region and world versions;
- streamed residency state;
- diagnostic explanations.

Representation-specific features remain available through typed capabilities rather than being forced into the lowest common denominator.

#### Runtime selection and composition

A world may mix representations. For example:

```text
Station floor              -> surface product
Elevator transition        -> semantic traversal link
Ventilation shaft crawler  -> narrow surface/graph product
Zero-G maintenance chamber -> volumetric product
Large NPC evacuation       -> hierarchical route + flow field
```

NAV compiles and coordinates these products so a route may cross representation boundaries through explicit typed transitions.

#### Performance and disabled cost

Unused representation families must not keep active schedulers, large caches, build stages, or shipping dependencies in a project that does not use them. The product/build manifest records which NAV representation modules and cooked artifacts are actually present.

#### Validation

Qualification requires equivalent semantic test cases across applicable representations: reachability, dynamic invalidation, links, streaming, agent profiles, deterministic/stable query behavior where promised, and diagnostics. Cross-representation transitions require dedicated fixtures.

#### Open implementation research

Not locked: exact navmesh generator; polygon representation; graph layout; voxel representation; flow-field algorithm; volumetric structure; spatial index; path-search family; or whether selected permissively licensed libraries are dependencies, forks, references, or replaced by Meridian-native implementations.

### Automatic-first navigation generation with explicit override `NAV-002` — *Normative*

NAV should derive usable navigation automatically from the authored world and agent requirements. Manual navigation authoring remains a precision and exception tool, not the normal prerequisite for basic pathfinding.

#### Authoring inputs

Automatic generation may consume typed source products from:

- Basalt terrain and large-world geometry;
- authored scene/world geometry;
- Cairn collision/collision intent products;
- doors, portals, elevators, ladders, rails, jump/climb links, and Smart Interaction metadata;
- moving-platform definitions;
- area volumes and environmental constraints;
- agent capability profiles;
- project-specific traversal annotations.

The source graph remains authoritative; the cooked navigation product is derived and rebuildable.

#### Default workflow

An ordinary workflow should be approximately:

```text
Create/import world
-> add character/agent profile
-> Navigation becomes available automatically
-> inspect only if something is wrong or needs custom behavior
```

The editor should surface generated navigation without forcing a separate bake ceremony every time a mesh moves.

#### Developer controls

Developers can explicitly:

- include/exclude surfaces;
- change traversal cost/semantic class;
- pin or forbid links;
- author special traversal transitions;
- set local generation resolution/error budgets;
- declare one-way or conditional traversal;
- mark regions as dynamically mutable;
- provide hand-authored navigation data where automatic generation is inappropriate;
- freeze/pin a generated product when required for production stability.

Overrides are source-controlled semantic data and survive regeneration.

#### Incrementality

Small authoring changes should invalidate only the relevant navigation regions/products. The asset/world compiler must explain why a region rebuilt and which source change triggered it.

#### Failure behavior

If automatic generation cannot confidently produce usable navigation, it should report the affected area and reason rather than silently making an important route disappear. Examples include impossible geometry, invalid scale, unsupported traversal topology, insufficient clearance, or contradictory annotations.

#### Qualification

Tests include common imported levels, terrain, stairs, ramps, narrow passages, doors, moving platforms, arbitrary gravity fixtures, 2D levels, huge streamed worlds, and deliberately malformed source. Automatic generation is evaluated on correctness, update latency, artifact size, stability under small edits, and ease of diagnosing failures.

### Incremental versioned navigation updates with immediate obstacle overlays `NAV-003` — *Normative*

Dynamic worlds use a two-speed update model: immediate cheap runtime changes can affect traversal before expensive structural navigation products finish rebuilding, while rebuilt navigation is published as an atomic versioned replacement.

#### Immediate path

For common temporary changes such as:

- a crate blocking a corridor;
- a closing door;
- moving characters;
- a vehicle parked across a route;
- temporary hazards or forbidden zones;

NAV may apply lightweight dynamic obstacle/cost/link state without rebuilding the structural navigation product.

#### Structural path

For changes such as:

- destroyed architecture;
- newly built structures;
- terrain excavation;
- persistent flooding changing traversability;
- a bridge or floor permanently removed;
- a newly created tunnel;

NAV schedules incremental regeneration of affected regions/products.

#### Versioning/publication

Queries execute against an explicit navigation snapshot/version. A replacement region is not half-published. Required data for the new version is validated and then atomically becomes queryable at an appropriate synchronization point.

Existing in-flight queries may finish against the older immutable snapshot. Callers can inspect the version associated with their result.

#### Path invalidation

An existing route carries enough provenance to determine whether its relevant regions/links changed. NAV can:

- keep the route when still valid;
- repair/refine only an affected segment;
- request a full replan;
- report a blocked state immediately when a dynamic overlay invalidates the next traversal.

#### Streaming interaction

A region may rebuild while unloaded or partially resident through headless navigation build products. The editor/game should not need to force-render a region to update its navigation data.

#### Failure and last-known-good

If a navigation rebuild fails, NAV retains the previous valid structural product where safe and keeps temporary dynamic blockers conservative. It must not publish corrupt/incomplete topology merely to remove a warning.

#### Observability

The editor/profiler should answer:

```text
Why did this path invalidate?
Which region is rebuilding?
Which obstacle currently blocks the route?
Which navigation version produced this result?
Why did this rebuild take 34 ms?
```

#### Open implementation research

Exact tile/region granularity, rebuild scheduler, snapshot reclamation scheme, local repair algorithm, and the relationship between navigation-region boundaries and Basalt runtime cells remain implementation decisions.

### Shared world data plus agent capability profiles `NAV-004` — *Normative*

NAV should not require a completely independent world bake for every character type when those agents share most of the same environment. The default model is shared navigation source/runtime data evaluated or specialized through typed agent capability profiles.

#### Agent profile semantics

An `AgentTraversalProfile` may define concepts such as:

- radius/footprint;
- standing and crouched height;
- maximum step;
- maximum slope;
- clearance requirements;
- walk/run/crawl/swim/fly/zero-G capabilities;
- jump/mantle/climb/ladder abilities;
- preferred/forbidden surface classes;
- door/interaction capabilities;
- turn radius and motion constraints where relevant;
- vehicle dimensions/capabilities;
- cost preferences.

These are semantic capabilities, not a promise that all pathfinding representations compute clearance identically.

#### Derived specialization

NAV may generate separate optimized runtime products for materially different profile families when that improves performance or correctness. For example, humanoid walking, heavy vehicle routing, and small-drone volumetric navigation may compile to different products while still sharing source identities and world semantics.

The key rule is that separate bakes/products are an optimization/domain requirement, not user-visible duplication of the entire world by default.

#### Dynamic profile state

Some capabilities may change at runtime:

- standing -> crouched;
- walking -> carrying bulky object;
- door access gained/lost;
- injured movement restrictions;
- vehicle attached/detached.

NAV can re-evaluate route validity/cost without pretending the underlying world geometry changed.

#### Bearings boundary

Bearings may choose among available capability states or goals; NAV determines geometric/traversal feasibility and route cost under the requested profile.

#### Qualification

Fixtures compare multiple agent profiles over the same world and test narrow passages, stairs, crouch routes, doors, vehicles, climbing transitions, arbitrary gravity, and streamed regions. The same stable semantic route should not require manually copied navigation authoring for each profile.

### Hierarchical long-distance path planning for streamed worlds `NAV-005` — *Normative*

Large-world routes must not require every fine navigation polygon/node across the entire path to be simultaneously resident. NAV supports hierarchical planning that can reason at coarse world scale and refine the route as relevant regions become available.

#### Hierarchy

A route may contain levels such as:

```text
World/sector route
-> region/portal sequence
-> local traversal corridor
-> fine path
-> local steering/avoidance
```

The exact number and representation of levels are not locked.

#### Streamed planning

The coarse graph carries enough connectivity/cost summary to answer long-distance planning questions even when fine data is unloaded. Basalt/world streaming can use route intent as a prefetch signal, while NAV consumes cell/residency information without owning general world streaming.

#### Refinement

Fine route sections are computed when their navigation products are resident or available headlessly. If a later refinement discovers that the coarse route is no longer feasible, NAV can repair/replan from an appropriate hierarchy level.

#### Dynamic worlds

Coarse connectivity summaries have explicit versions and can be invalidated by structural world changes. A destroyed bridge should invalidate the relevant world-scale edge without requiring immediate fine traversal loading across the full world.

#### Multiple targets and route queries

The hierarchy should support not only `A -> B` shortest paths but future queries such as:

- reachable region sets;
- route alternatives;
- cost-to-area fields;
- evacuation/flow planning;
- nearest valid destination;
- tactical route candidates requested by Bearings.

NAV still returns traversal facts/candidates; Bearings decides why one candidate is tactically preferable.

#### Qualification

Tests include 10 km, 100 km, orbital/station-scale, disconnected regions, streamed/unloaded sections, teleport/elevator/portal edges, moving transport links, and dynamic topology changes. Metrics include path latency, memory, fine-data residency demand, route repair latency, and explainability.

### NAV owns local geometric avoidance; Bearings owns tactical choice `NAV-006` — *Normative*

Local collision-aware movement and high-level agent decision-making are deliberately separated.

#### NAV owns

- geometric short-horizon avoidance;
- keeping an agent inside traversable space;
- avoiding dynamic obstacles/other agents under the requested movement constraints;
- local velocity/path corridor feasibility;
- collision-free candidate velocities/steering outputs where the selected avoidance implementation supports them;
- reporting when local avoidance cannot satisfy the requested route.

#### Bearings/gameplay own

- whether an agent yields or pushes forward;
- who has social/mission priority;
- flanking;
- chasing or disengaging;
- hiding;
- formation/tactical goals;
- intentionally blocking another actor;
- abandoning one route for another objective;
- personality/game-rule decisions.

#### Interface principle

Bearings asks something like:

```text
Move toward this route/goal under these tactical constraints.
```

NAV can return:

```text
locally feasible motion
blocked
slow/costly
alternate local corridor
collision/avoidance conflict
```

It does not independently decide that an NPC is frightened and should flee.

#### Group motion

Future crowd/formation systems may involve both authorities. NAV may compute collision-free/flow-compatible movement fields, while Bearings assigns groups, formation objectives, lane preference, social rules, or tactical behavior.

#### Failure

If no local solution exists, NAV reports the geometric reason and bounded alternatives instead of silently steering the character away from its strategic intent indefinitely.

#### Qualification

Test dense crowds, opposing flows, door bottlenecks, narrow corridors, static/dynamic obstacles, multiple agent sizes, moving platforms, low frame rates, deterministic/replay profiles, and path/avoidance interaction under network authority.

### First-class oriented-surface and volumetric navigation in the complete architecture `NAV-007` — *Normative*

NAV's architecture must not hard-code global `+Y`/world-up walking as the universal meaning of traversal. Conventional ground navigation remains the simplest and earliest implementation, while the complete system supports navigation on arbitrarily oriented surfaces and through 3D volumes.

#### Oriented surfaces

A traversable surface may have a local frame or gravity/down field supplied through Meridian world/physics contracts. This enables:

- walls and ceilings;
- spherical/planetary surfaces;
- rotating habitats;
- arbitrary local gravity;
- gravity handoff regions;
- characters walking around small bodies or station structures.

NAV should reason about connectivity and orientation transitions explicitly rather than projecting everything onto a world-up plane.

#### Volumetric traversal

Free-space products may support:

- flight;
- swimming;
- zero-G movement;
- underwater volumes;
- drones;
- other unconstrained 3D movement.

The exact data structure and solver are open.

#### Cairn/Artus integration

NAV provides feasible routes/trajectory corridors under an agent's movement capabilities. Cairn remains the physical truth and may reject or constrain motion. Artus adapts articulated body movement to the achieved traversal. Persistent mismatch can trigger NAV re-evaluation/replanning through explicit feedback rather than hidden subsystem reach-through.

#### Authoring

Developers can inspect local navigation frames, surface orientation, gravity influence, transition edges, and volumetric connectivity. Ordinary world-up games should not need to configure any of this manually.

#### Staged delivery

This lock does **not** require volumetric and arbitrary-gravity navigation to block the first usable NAV release. The implementation order may be:

```text
ordinary 2D/3D ground navigation
-> dynamic updates/hierarchy
-> special links/moving surfaces
-> arbitrary-oriented surfaces
-> volumetric navigation
-> advanced mixed-domain traversal
```

The architecture and serialized semantics must simply avoid making the later stages a rewrite.

#### Qualification

Future qualification includes normal ground worlds, spherical gravity, wall/ceiling traversal, rotating frames, zero-G chambers, swim/fly volumes, transitions between surface and volume traversal, and large-world streaming.

### NAV explicit non-goals and open implementation work — *Open implementation research*

The product contract intentionally leaves open:

- exact pathfinding/search algorithms;
- exact navmesh generation library or in-house implementation;
- polygonization/voxelization resolution strategy;
- region/tile size;
- path smoothing/funnel implementation;
- exact cost model syntax;
- query API and snapshot types;
- dynamic obstacle algorithm;
- crowd avoidance algorithm;
- flow-field representation;
- semantic/off-mesh link source format;
- determinism guarantees;
- networking/replication of navigation state;
- server/client navigation authority;
- cache/storage compression;
- GPU acceleration;
- exact world-cell/NAV-region mapping;
- exact editor navigation workspace;
- exact testing thresholds.

Those are suitable for evidence-driven NAV prototypes and qualification.

---

The following NAV contract defines how callers use NAV, how semantic traversal/costs are represented, how moving frames and multiplayer affect navigation, how crowd-scale movement fits the authority model, and how an automatic system remains diagnosable. Exact algorithms remain evidence-driven implementation choices.

### Unified semantic query API over versioned snapshots `NAV-008` — *Normative*

NAV exposes one conceptual query family for pathfinding, reachability, nearest traversable point/region, cost estimation, corridor/segment tests, approach-region queries, and related traversal questions. Callers do not need separate public APIs merely because one execution is synchronous and another is scheduled.

The normal read model is an immutable/versioned NAV snapshot. Cheap queries may execute immediately when the caller is already in a phase that can safely read the authoritative snapshot. Expensive queries may be scheduled/batched automatically or explicitly without changing their semantic result type. Results carry the NAV version used so gameplay/Bearings can detect stale assumptions after a world update.

The final API must support cancellation, deadlines/budgets, structured failure reasons, query tracing, and deterministic/replay-qualified modes where required. No public query may accidentally force a global NAV rebuild or wait on mutable authoring state.

### Typed semantic cost layers `NAV-009` — *Normative*

NAV supports compiled semantic cost layers rather than either geometric distance only or arbitrary scripting callbacks in the hot search loop. Built-in/project-defined semantics may represent road quality, mud, water, hazards, doors, noise, exposure, crowd density, slope/energy, destructibility, traversal permissions, or game-specific concepts.

Agent capability/profiles assign costs or prohibitions to layers, and runtime systems may publish bounded versioned cost overlays. Bearings/gameplay may change preferences/goals without becoming the path-search implementation. Custom cost logic compiles into typed/batchable data where possible; arbitrary per-edge script calls are an expert escape hatch only if a later benchmark proves a safe need.

Costs remain explainable: path diagnostics can attribute route choice to distance, semantic layers, capabilities, dynamic overlays, and hierarchy decisions.

### Semantic Traversal Links `NAV-010` — *Normative*

Special movement between ordinary traversable regions uses typed Traversal Links. Candidate categories include doors, jumps, mantles, ladders, elevators, teleporters, climbing transitions, vehicle entry/exit, gravity transitions, and project-defined actions.

A link describes feasibility, required agent capabilities, approach/exit regions, timing/cost information, dynamic availability, and the semantic action required. NAV owns connectivity and route feasibility; Artus/Cairn/gameplay perform the actual interaction or movement and report success/failure.

Links may be authored, generated from Smart Interaction/world metadata, or proposed by runtime/editor inference. Automatic inference is allowed to create/validate link candidates but does not erase explicit author control for important traversal.

### Navigation regions with moving/local reference frames `NAV-011` — *Normative*

NAV regions may live in local coordinate frames so elevators, trains, ships, rotating structures, large vehicles, moving platforms, arbitrary-gravity environments, and other mobile spaces do not require continuous full rebakes in world coordinates.

Connectivity between frames is explicit and versioned. A moving region can retain internal topology while its transforms/portals relative to other frames change. Simple projects may still compile basic moving-platform behavior into traversal links without exposing frame machinery.

Basalt/world coordinates remain the durable world identity; Cairn owns physical transforms/motion; NAV owns traversal connectivity in/among navigation frames. Frame changes must integrate with streaming, server simulation, replay, and large-world precision without making a moving vehicle a separate hidden world.

### Multiplayer navigation authority profiles `NAV-012` — *Normative*

Gameplay-critical navigation is server/host authoritative by default for authoritative agents, while clients may compute local paths for visualization, interpolation, prediction, or non-authoritative agents. NAV data normally derives from the same cooked/versioned world products rather than being continuously replicated as raw navmeshes.

Meridian's network topology profile may choose among transmitting compact route/corridor results, replicating goals plus authoritative world state and recomputing paths, or hybrid approaches. The engine does not force one packet strategy across co-op, competitive, rollback, deterministic strategy, and custom networking profiles.

Navigation results used for authoritative gameplay carry stable agent/world/link identities and version information. Host migration, replay, save restoration, and streamed-world promotion must not depend on process-local NAV pointers.

### Staged first-party crowd-routing toolkit `NAV-013` — *Normative*

The complete NAV vision includes more than pairwise collision avoidance. First-party crowd tooling may include local avoidance, density/congestion fields, bottleneck handling, flow fields, lane tendencies, shared-route optimization, group traversal primitives, and large-population cost representations.

Bearings owns group intent, tactics, social/behavior decisions, formations as goals, yielding policy, pursuit/flee choices, and other semantic decisions. NAV owns geometric feasibility and efficient crowd motion under those requests.

Delivery is staged: robust local avoidance and flow/shared-destination tools can arrive before sophisticated congestion/lane/group optimization. Crowd systems must degrade by representation tier rather than requiring one expensive per-agent solver for thousands of agents.

### NAV path-causality and explanation suite `NAV-014` — *Normative*

NAV must be able to explain reachability, route choice, route invalidation, high-cost corridors, stuck agents, failed capabilities, congestion, avoidance decisions, and rebuild/publication state. A green-navmesh overlay alone is not sufficient for an automatic multi-representation system.

The editor can visualize representation hierarchy, traversable regions, clearance, semantic costs, capability constraints, Traversal Links, obstacles, moving frames, streamed/unloaded regions, snapshot versions, alternative routes, avoidance/crowd fields, incremental rebuilds, and query timings.

Development traces record bounded query and path causality so a developer can inspect which world/NAV version was queried, why alternatives lost, which semantic costs dominated, and what changed when a path invalidated. The complete vision is the explanation suite; early milestones may begin with strong conventional overlays before all causality UI is implemented.

### NAV unresolved implementation work — *Open implementation research*

Open implementation work: path-search algorithms and data structures; snapshot storage/layout; sync-vs-async thresholds; cost-layer encoding and composition; link-generation algorithms; moving-frame topology update math; deterministic navigation level; client/server route encoding; crowd solver(s); GPU acceleration; query cache policy; exact editor workspace; and concrete performance/quality thresholds. These are prototype/evidence questions unless they materially alter the user-facing contract.

---

This main-engine specification does **not** finalize or authorize the separate Meridian AI model/runtime/training program. The first-party TemperTally model/training program remains a separate non-blocking program; the AI-neutral semantic agent foundation is part of the main 1.0 implementation program. AI-neutral APIs, transactions, observability, source-control services, profiling, extension boundaries and recovery may be implemented earlier because they are general Meridian infrastructure, not because AI is required.


## Detailed Bearings game-agent intelligence contract


### Ease-of-use condition inherited from PRODUCT-002 — *Normative*

Every Bearings capability below is conditional on ordinary NPC creation remaining easier than comparable workflows in Unity, Godot, and GameMaker. Advanced planning architecture is not permission to make a beginner manually construct a planner stack.

The intended ordinary workflow should converge toward something like:

```text
Add Agent / Character Intelligence
-> choose or accept a Behavior Profile
-> choose goals/role or a starter behavior
-> connect a character/controller automatically
-> Play
```

A profile/template may automatically configure perception, knowledge storage, common actions, planning limits, group participation, NAV/Artus integration, determinism policy, and performance budgets. The exact profile schema remains implementation work; the **requirement that a simple path exists is already locked**.

Advanced developers can inspect and override goals, utility scores, action schemas, planner bounds, fact lifetimes, sensors, group hierarchy, scheduling, and debugging traces. Easy defaults and advanced depth must coexist.

### Hybrid goals/utility plus bounded planning `BEAR-001` — *Normative*

Bearings does not make one authoring formalism universal. Its normal architecture combines:

1. **goals** describing what an agent is trying to achieve or maintain;
2. **utility/scoring** for choosing among immediately meaningful alternatives;
3. **bounded plans/task structures** when an objective requires multiple dependent actions;
4. optional explicit authored task/behavior structures where precision matters.

A simple guard can be expressed without a planner search over a giant action universe:

```text
Goals
- remain alive
- guard entrance
- investigate meaningful disturbance

Candidate responses
- continue patrol
- investigate
- call for help
- use cover
- retreat
```

Utility evaluates relevant alternatives from the agent's current knowledge and role. When an action expands into a multi-step problem, Bearings can invoke the bounded planner described by `BEAR-004`.

#### Boundary

Behavior trees may still exist as an optional authoring/runtime representation for explicit sequences, imported content, or projects that prefer them. `BEAR-001` rejects making a behavior tree the mandatory universal AI substrate.

Likewise, utility scoring does not own path feasibility, physical interaction, animation, or gameplay consequences. It chooses semantic intent/actions; other subsystem contracts execute or validate them.

#### Ease requirement

Starter roles such as Patrol, Guard, Follow, Passive NPC, Search/Investigate, Creature, Squad Member, or Custom should be able to configure common goals/actions automatically. Users should not have to understand utility theory before making a guard walk around and react to the player.

#### Qualification

Test at minimum: simple patrol, stealth guard, creature chase/flee, civilian/reactive NPC, tactical squad member, strategy-like worker, and noncombat interaction agents. The hybrid model loses if common cases require more manual conceptual setup than an equivalent conventional behavior-tree workflow.

### Per-agent knowledge with explicit provenance/confidence and optional shared layers `BEAR-002` — *Normative*

Agents should normally decide from what they **know or believe**, not by directly querying omniscient world truth for every decision.

A Bearings fact/observation can carry semantic information such as:

```text
subject / fact kind
value or estimated state
source
observed time
confidence
spatial uncertainty where relevant
expiry/decay policy
visibility/sharing policy
```

Examples:

- saw the player near a doorway;
- heard an impact behind a wall;
- knows a door was locked when last checked;
- ally reported an enemy in another region;
- remembers a useful object location;
- believes a route is dangerous.

#### Shared knowledge

Individual knowledge remains distinct from optional squad/faction/team knowledge. Sharing can be immediate, delayed, communication-dependent, lossy, filtered by role, or disabled by the project.

A squad should not automatically become telepathic merely because every member uses Bearings.

#### Ground truth

Gameplay and subsystem state remain authoritative truth. Bearings knowledge is an agent-facing semantic representation that may be stale, uncertain, incomplete, or wrong. Specific game mechanics may explicitly grant perfect knowledge.

#### Open implementation choices

Exact fact schemas, decay models, spatial uncertainty representation, memory capacity/compaction, communication channels, and authoring UX remain to be decided.

### First-party extensible perception framework `BEAR-003` — *Normative*

Bearings provides optimized first-party perception/sensing rather than forcing every game to rebuild sight/hearing/proximity logic. Projects can add custom semantic senses through the same typed observation contract.

Candidate first-party senses include:

- visibility/sight;
- hearing/acoustic events;
- proximity/contact awareness;
- damage/threat awareness;
- interaction/object awareness;
- environmental state awareness when relevant.

#### Cross-subsystem integration

This decision is an explicit application of `SUBSYS-005`. Sensors should consume the best semantic information already produced elsewhere instead of reimplementing unrelated engines inside Bearings.

Examples:

- **Penumbra / world visibility** may provide visibility/occlusion-relevant products where appropriate, while gameplay can still define stealth visibility rules;
- **Wavefront/acoustic world** can inform audible propagation or semantic sound events;
- **Isobar** can reduce visibility or alter environmental perception through fog/weather state;
- **Torsant** can publish fire/smoke/heat/hazard observations;
- **Cairn** can provide collision/contact/physical-event facts;
- **NAV** can provide reachable/route/traversal facts;
- **Artus** can expose semantic character posture/interaction state where another agent could actually perceive it;
- gameplay can publish arbitrary semantic events.

No integration may bypass subsystem authority or create mandatory recurring work when the relevant sensor/capability is disabled.

#### Custom senses

A custom sensor publishes typed observations/facts with declared cost, update policy, and provenance. Arbitrary scripting callbacks inside every perception hot loop are not the default execution model; compiled/batched paths should remain possible.

### Bounded hierarchical planning `BEAR-004` — *Normative*

Bearings supports multi-step planning, but planning is deliberately **bounded and structured**, not an unconstrained search over every action an agent might theoretically perform.

A high-level goal may select an authored strategy/template and fill in context-dependent steps:

```text
Goal: reach secure room
Strategy: enter secure area
- find suitable entrance
- if blocked, choose allowed resolution
- acquire route
- traverse
- confirm arrival/secure state
```

The planner can adapt among available semantic actions while respecting budgets, priorities, hard preconditions, game rules, and deterministic/stable policies.

#### Bounds

Plans must have explicit limits such as search depth, expansions, time/CPU budget, allowed action domains, replanning triggers, and fallback behavior. A low-priority NPC cannot create an unbounded frame hitch because a goal became complicated.

#### Hierarchy

Planning may occur at multiple semantic levels: choose strategy, expand subgoal, choose action, ask NAV for routes, then hand movement to Artus/Cairn. The exact planner algorithm is evidence-driven and not locked here.

#### Failure

If no plan fits the budget, Bearings returns a typed reason and can choose a fallback goal/strategy, continue a current safe behavior, request more computation later, or become deliberately idle. Silent runaway search is forbidden.

### Optional hierarchical agents for squads/groups/organizations `BEAR-005` — *Normative*

Bearings can represent decision-makers above individual characters when a game benefits from them. Examples include squads, crowds/groups, factions, work teams, organizations, or strategy-game formations.

A group-level agent may choose shared objectives/constraints:

```text
Squad objective: contain target
- member A: hold exit
- member B: flank
- member C: suppress / observe
```

Individual agents still retain their own knowledge, local needs, perception, movement feasibility, and execution state.

#### Optionality

A small game using ten independent NPCs does not initialize a faction/squad hierarchy merely because Bearings supports it. Group-agent capabilities must satisfy the engine-wide effectively-zero-disabled-cost rule.

#### Shared abstractions, not forced identical algorithms

The same broad goal/action/fact vocabulary can span levels, but a faction planner does not have to run the identical algorithm or tick frequency as a character agent.

#### Open implementation choices and later evidence

Group knowledge propagation, role assignment, formation ownership, crowd-vs-squad split, hierarchical scheduling, and group plan conflict resolution remain open.

### Rich first-party semantic action library plus project-defined actions `BEAR-006` — *Normative*

Meridian ships reusable semantic actions so projects do not need to rebuild basic agent behaviors from scratch, while avoiding a genre-specific hardcoded AI vocabulary.

Candidate common actions include:

- MoveTo / Follow / Approach;
- LookAt / Observe;
- Wait;
- Interact;
- Patrol;
- Guard;
- SearchArea / Investigate;
- MaintainDistance;
- Flee / Withdraw;
- UseCover where a project enables cover semantics;
- FollowFormation / MoveWithGroup;
- communicate/share observation;
- project-configurable combinations of NAV traversal and Artus Smart Interactions.

Projects can define additional typed semantic actions without modifying Bearings itself.

#### Action contract

An action should eventually declare at least its semantic inputs, required capabilities, preconditions, expected effects/outcomes, execution owner, cancellation/interrupt behavior, observability/debug label, networking relevance, and cost/budget class. Exact schema remains implementation work.

#### Ownership

Bearings chooses/coordinates an action; it does not absorb the subsystem that performs it. `MoveTo` uses NAV and movement/controller/Artus contracts. `Interact` can use Artus Smart Interactions and gameplay authority. `Wait` needs neither. A project action can call a typed gameplay command.

### Explicit determinism profiles; Stable is the default `BEAR-007` — *Normative*

Bearings exposes explicit decision determinism profiles rather than imposing strict bit-identical behavior or accepting hidden nondeterminism everywhere.

Current conceptual profiles:

- **Fast** — favors throughput/parallelism; exact decision identity may vary where semantically acceptable;
- **Stable — DEFAULT** — normal Meridian behavior; seeded randomness, stable ordering, reproducible-enough decision behavior, controlled concurrency effects, and strong debugging/replay usefulness without paying the full cost of strict determinism;
- **Deterministic** — tighter reproducibility guarantees suitable for deterministic simulation/network/replay requirements;
- **Strict** — strongest qualified constraints, potentially limiting algorithms/parallelism and requiring explicit compatibility evidence.

The exact formal guarantees of each profile still require implementation research and must align with Cairn, gameplay simulation, networking, save/replay, and task scheduling.

#### Randomness

Bearings randomness must come from explicit scoped/seeded sources. Hidden process-global RNG use that makes debugging or replay depend on unrelated call order is not acceptable.

#### Stable default meaning

Stable does **not** mean every floating-point intermediate or worker schedule must be byte-identical. It means ordinary projects should get predictable, explainable, testable behavior and stable semantic outcomes whenever the selected algorithms can reasonably provide them.

### Integration-matrix highlights

The complete `SUBSYS-005` matrix remains maintained separately, but the Bearings contract establishes these relationships:

| System | Bearings relationship |
|---|---|
| NAV | Bearings chooses goals/tactics; NAV owns feasibility, path/cost and local geometric avoidance. |
| Artus | Bearings emits semantic motion/interaction intent; Artus performs body motion and interactions. |
| Cairn | Physical events become observations; Cairn owns physical truth. Bearings never directly mutates solver state as “AI.” |
| Wavefront | Semantic/acoustic events can drive hearing; Bearings does not run its own audio propagation engine. |
| Isobar | Weather/visibility/environment state can affect senses, costs and goals through typed context. |
| Torsant | Fire/smoke/heat/fluid hazards can become observations/costs and planning constraints. |
| Basalt/world streaming | Agent knowledge/plans use durable world/region identity; Bearings does not own cell residency. Coarse off-screen agent state must cooperate with world tiers. |
| Alluvium | Procedural authoring may generate/annotate AI-relevant semantic regions/actions; runtime authority remains with Bearings/gameplay/NAV as appropriate. |
| Penumbra | Rendering is not game-AI truth; visibility-related products may contribute to perception only through qualified semantic contracts. |
| Meridian UI/editor | Behavior/profile authoring, knowledge inspection, planner traces and tuning use Meridian UI transactions. |
| Networking | `BEAR-012` owns server-authoritative defaults and explicit presentation/prediction profiles; replicated decision state is semantic and bounded. |
| Save/persistence | Typed persistence scopes retain durable goals, facts, roles, and required action state; transient planner caches and traces remain derived unless explicitly declared durable. |
| Diagnostics | Decision causality must integrate into the global trace/explanation vocabulary. |

### Bearings — *Normative*

#### Profile-first NPC authoring that remains directly editable `BEAR-008` — *Normative*

The normal workflow is **Behavior Profile first**. Adding `Character Intelligence` (user-facing naming subject to editor design) offers compact first-party profiles such as Guard, Passive NPC, Companion, Creature, Worker/Civilian, or Custom. Profiles configure sensible defaults for goals, perception, memory, action sets, NAV/Artus integration, decision budgets, cognition tier policy, and determinism without requiring the user to construct a planner, blackboard, perception graph, or action scheduler manually.

This convenience has a hard editability requirement: a developer must be able to understand and edit the resulting behavior through the editor **without AI and without reading documentation for ordinary changes**. Relevant goals, senses, facts, action settings, and planner/tier parameters appear through discoverable inspectors/workspaces. Advanced graph/planner internals may be progressively disclosed, but the profile may not become an opaque blob.

Profile-managed values, project overrides, and fully custom/detached behavior state must be distinguished so Meridian never silently overwrites deliberate edits. Common edits such as changing patrol behavior, sight/hearing range, priorities, allowed actions, reactions, or group role should be obvious from the normal editor surface.

#### Semantic fact memory with confidence, age, decay and controlled sharing `BEAR-009` — *Normative*

Bearings agents primarily reason from semantic facts/observations rather than querying omniscient live truth for every decision. Facts can carry source, timestamp/age, confidence, expiry/decay policy, semantic subject/object identity, location/region, and provenance.

Examples include last-seen position, heard event, observed hazard, known door state, ally status, suspected target region, or remembered interaction result. Some facts remain exact until invalidated; others decay or become uncertain. The exact decay functions are implementation/tuning details.

Agents may share selected facts through explicit squad/faction/communication rules, but shared knowledge is not automatically telepathic. Rich episodic memory remains an optional later capability rather than a required baseline representation.

#### One typed asynchronous semantic action lifecycle `BEAR-010` — *Normative*

Bearings actions share one semantic execution lifecycle even when different subsystems perform the work. The contract supports states equivalent to Requested, Starting, Running, Blocked, Succeeded, Failed, Cancelled, and Interrupted, plus progress/status and typed failure/block reasons where useful.

Actions declare their execution owner and interruption/cancellation semantics. `MoveTo` may be executed by NAV/controller/Artus; `Interact` may use Artus Smart Interactions and gameplay; a project action may invoke project gameplay code. Bearings coordinates and observes the lifecycle rather than absorbing those systems.

The contract must support long-running actions, cancellation on goal changes, temporary blocking, replanning, save/network classification, diagnostics, and deterministic/stable replay where required.

#### Automatic cognition tiers for scale `BEAR-011` — *Normative*

Bearings automatically scales cognition through representation tiers rather than forcing every NPC to run full perception/planning at the same rate. Conceptual tiers may include Dormant, Aggregate, Reactive, Planning, and Full, though exact names/count are implementation details.

Tier choice considers visibility, distance, gameplay importance, player/network relevance, current interaction, group role, world-streaming state, and global CPU budgets. Lower tiers may reduce sense frequency, utility evaluation, planner use, memory maintenance, action detail, or articulated integration while preserving durable goals, role, important knowledge, and semantic state needed for promotion.

Promotion/demotion must avoid obvious discontinuities and must cooperate with Artus motion LOD, NAV/world tiers, networking, save state, and the performance governor. Developer overrides exist, but manual per-distance tuning is not the normal workflow.

#### Multiplayer Bearings profiles, hidden behind advanced controls `BEAR-012` — *Normative*

Normal multiplayer uses **Server Authoritative** Bearings behavior: the server/host owns gameplay-relevant goals, plans, knowledge, decisions, and action state; clients receive the semantic state needed for presentation and prediction.

Advanced projects may select qualified profiles such as Deterministic Shared, Local/Presentation, or Custom when their topology requires it. These profiles are **not part of the beginner/default surface**; they live behind advanced networking/AI settings so ordinary users do not have to understand authority models just to create an NPC.

The replication schema distinguishes gameplay-authoritative knowledge/decision state from presentation-only local behavior. Host migration, rollback/deterministic modes, save/replay, and anti-cheat/server validation use those classifications rather than serializing arbitrary planner memory blindly.

#### Bounded decision-causality timeline and explanation suite `BEAR-013` — *Normative*

Bearings provides a bounded semantic trace capable of explaining why an agent acted, did not act, replanned, became blocked, changed goals, or accepted/rejected information. The editor can align perception, fact-memory changes, goals/utility, planning steps, group orders, NAV results, action lifecycle, cognition tier changes, networking corrections, and performance cost.

Useful questions include “why didn't this NPC attack?”, “why did it investigate that sound?”, “what did it know then?”, “why was this action unavailable?”, and “which fact caused the replan?”. Explanations point to raw semantic evidence rather than inventing narrative rationales.

Tracing is bounded/quality-configurable so large crowds do not retain unlimited histories. Explicit capture modes may preserve longer sessions for debugging and regression tests.

#### Typed semantic context/fact ingress from the rest of Meridian `BEAR-014` — *Normative*

Automatic Bearings integration uses typed semantic observations/context rather than a global dynamic blackboard or Bearings reaching into every subsystem's private state. Relevant systems can publish facts/events such as audible events, visibility/fog changes, hazards, physical impacts, route failures, character interaction states, world-region changes, or gameplay semantics.

Direct subsystem queries remain available for deliberate expensive questions, but ordinary perception/context should reuse semantic products already computed elsewhere when valid. Every ingress type records ownership/provenance, update/expiry policy, cost/budget class, and whether it represents authoritative truth, an observation, or derived agent knowledge.

This contract is an important implementation of `SUBSYS-006`: first-party systems should cooperate without duplicating audio propagation, visibility reasoning, hazard classification, route feasibility, or body-interaction semantics inside Bearings.

The Bearings product architecture is complete for this specification. Remaining items are implementation/evidence work unless a prototype exposes a contradiction. These include exact utility equations, planner algorithm/indexing, fact storage/decay implementation, profile schema, cognition-tier thresholds, action executor internals, replication packet layout, deterministic guarantees, group scheduling, and trace-storage format.

The ease gate remains binding: a normal NPC workflow must remain discoverable and editable without AI or documentation, even as advanced systems grow underneath it.

---


## Balanced user-mode protection contract

### Purpose and product boundary `PROTECT-001` — *Normative*

Meridian provides an **optional, balanced, first-party user-mode protection capability** for games that need more than ordinary package signing and server validation but do not want an invasive kernel anti-cheat product.

Its purpose is to:

- make common tampering, malformed clients, trivial injection, unauthorized module loading, replay manipulation, impossible-state submission, and obvious automation materially harder;
- give small and medium teams safer defaults without requiring them to build a security platform from scratch;
- correlate client integrity evidence with authoritative server behavior;
- expose provider-neutral integration points for external user-mode/platform services;
- remain inspectable, removable, privacy-conscious, mod-compatible by declared policy, and honest about its limitations.

It is **not** DRM, a promise of secrecy for code distributed to players, a global Meridian ban service, a mandatory online dependency, or a claim that a hostile machine can be made trustworthy.

### Permanent exclusions `PROTECT-002` — *Normative*

First-party Meridian protection MUST NOT include or require:

- a kernel driver, hypervisor component, boot-time component, or similarly privileged anti-cheat agent;
- a persistent system-wide privileged daemon unrelated to the running game;
- broad scanning of unrelated files, browser history, private documents, or unrelated process memory;
- mandatory telemetry, a mandatory Meridian account, or mandatory Dead Signal Works infrastructure;
- always-online checks for games that do not otherwise require networking;
- one opaque signal directly causing a permanent sanction;
- a hidden cross-game identity or global ban list operated by Meridian;
- security-through-obscurity claims that distributed client code or content is secret;
- deliberate incompatibility with accessibility software merely because it injects input, overlays information, or uses assistive APIs;
- silent disabling of mods, debuggers, overlays, capture tools, or development workflows without an explicit selected policy.

A third party may build unrelated privileged software using ordinary native operating-system facilities, but that does not become a supported Meridian protection path merely because Meridian is open source.

### Capability profiles `PROTECT-003` — *Normative*

The normal product exposes a small set of semantic profiles rather than a wall of low-level switches. Exact labels may evolve, but the behavior classes are:

1. **Disabled**
   - no protection-specific runtime host, recurring task, listener, telemetry, package chunk, startup scan, integrity challenge, or editor surface ships;
   - ordinary signing, package verification, save recovery, protocol validation, and secure coding remain available because they are general engine facilities.

2. **Standard Multiplayer**
   - authoritative server validation;
   - generated protocol/schema/range/rate validation;
   - signed package/module manifest verification;
   - bounded runtime integrity checks around Meridian-owned modules and declared extension boundaries;
   - impossible-state and suspicious-behavior signals;
   - replayable server-side evidence and diagnostics;
   - permissive compatibility with declared mods and common overlays by policy.

3. **Competitive User-Mode**
   - everything in Standard Multiplayer;
   - stricter approved-module and package-origin policy;
   - stronger challenge/response freshness checks;
   - qualified user-mode anti-tamper, anti-injection, and anti-debug measures where platform policy, accessibility, stability, and false-positive evidence permit them;
   - stricter evidence correlation and protective-action policy;
   - explicit unsupported-platform/fallback behavior.

4. **Development / Mod-Friendly**
   - preserves server validation and package provenance while allowing declared debuggers, unsigned local modules, development consoles, overlays, hot reload, and mod workspaces;
   - cannot accidentally be published as a competitive release without a visible Release diagnostic and policy review.

Projects may define advanced profiles, but profiles are validated semantic policy documents rather than arbitrary scripts with ambient authority.

### Authority boundaries `PROTECT-004` — *Normative*

Protection is deliberately split across existing owners:

| Concern | Authority |
|---|---|
| Game rules, valid commands, impossible states, simulation authority | Gameplay + NET server authority |
| Package/module identity, signing, update trust, provenance, key policy | SEC + Build/Release |
| Client-side bounded integrity collection and correlation contract | Protection capability |
| Accounts, reports, moderation cases, sanctions, appeal workflows | Collective/provider adapters when selected |
| Mods, allowed extensions, capability grants, package overlays | MOD/Package Lab + project policy |
| Platform attestation or store-native trust signals | Platform-service adapters |
| Accessibility compatibility policy | Project + Accessibility + protection review |

The protection subsystem may consume evidence from these authorities. It does not duplicate their source truth or silently take over their decisions.

### Threat model and honesty `PROTECT-005` — *Normative*

The baseline threat model includes:

- a modified or instrumented client process;
- altered package/module data;
- unauthorized native or managed modules;
- malformed, replayed, reordered, duplicated, rate-abusive, or impossible network commands;
- local save/config manipulation where a game declares integrity relevance;
- automation/bot behavior visible through game semantics;
- debugger/injection tools targeting the running game;
- compromised third-party plugins or provider SDKs;
- stale or forged integrity evidence;
- malicious servers falsely accusing clients;
- false positives caused by accessibility tools, overlays, capture software, emulators, compatibility layers, unusual devices, or platform updates.

Meridian MUST state plainly that a determined attacker controlling a player machine can inspect, copy, modify, emulate, and eventually bypass many user-mode defenses. Client evidence raises cost and improves correlation; it does not replace server authority.

### Signed content and approved-module policy `PROTECT-006` — *Normative*

Release products may carry a signed manifest describing executable modules, managed assemblies, bytecode, shaders where relevant, native libraries, package chunks, mod overlays, configuration classes, and declared extension points.

Verification rules:

- hashes/signatures bind exact release identity and package role;
- mutable player data is never confused with signed installed content;
- allowed mods and extension packages are represented explicitly rather than by disabling all verification;
- development builds may trust local keys or unsigned content under a visible development profile;
- missing, altered, stale, or extra modules produce typed evidence, not an unconditional permanent ban;
- platform/store wrapping, patching, code signing, notarization, anti-malware transformation, and compatibility layers are accounted for by target-specific qualification;
- verification failures retain enough safe detail for support without publishing exploit-enabling internals.

### Runtime integrity and challenge/response `PROTECT-007` — *Normative direction*

Where qualified, the client may perform bounded user-mode checks such as:

- verifying loaded Meridian-owned modules against the release manifest;
- checking selected read-only code/data regions or control metadata;
- validating critical configuration provenance;
- detecting selected unsupported debugger/injection/tamper states;
- responding to server challenges that prove possession of fresh release-bound state;
- measuring internal consistency between independently derived values;
- confirming that required protection components remain active for the selected profile.

Checks MUST be:

- bounded in CPU, memory, I/O, startup, and latency cost;
- platform-specific behind Meridian-owned evidence contracts;
- resilient to ordinary OS updates and compatibility layers;
- cancelable or degradable according to declared policy;
- incapable of gaining authority outside the running game and its approved resources;
- safe when unavailable: `UnsupportedCapability`, `Unavailable`, `Degraded`, and `DeniedByUserOrPlatform` remain first-class outcomes.

A challenge implementation is an interchangeable strategy. The durable contract is freshness, provenance, scope, evidence quality, and declared fallback.

### Server-authoritative validation `PROTECT-008` — *Normative*

The strongest default protection remains authoritative game/server validation.

Meridian should generate or assist with:

- command/state schema validation;
- numeric ranges, enum validity, identity ownership, authority, sequence, epoch, and freshness checks;
- rate and budget limits;
- impossible transition detection;
- server-side physics/gameplay plausibility hooks;
- inventory/economy transaction validation;
- replay/message-order validation;
- prediction-versus-authority correction evidence;
- content/mod compatibility checks;
- deterministic or bounded-tolerance verification where the game selects it.

Generated validation is inspectable and extendable. It may not be treated as sufficient merely because code was generated; real adversarial fixtures and game-specific invariants are still required.

### Behavioral and impossible-state evidence `PROTECT-009` — *Normative direction*

Protection may collect project-declared semantic observations such as impossible movement, command timing, action rates, economic inconsistencies, hidden-information use, repeated prediction divergence, or invalid content state.

Every signal carries:

```text
signal identity
source and collection authority
subject/session identity
observation window
confidence and limitations
release/policy revision
provenance and freshness
privacy/retention class
alternative explanations
correlation references
```

Rules:

- one signal is not automatically guilt;
- models/rules are versioned and testable;
- serious sanctions require the game's declared review/appeal policy;
- protective actions may be temporary and reversible while evidence is reviewed;
- evidence must distinguish malicious behavior from lag, device faults, accessibility tools, bugs, platform limitations, and server faults;
- the game, not Meridian, defines competitive rules and acceptable modifications.

### Protective actions `PROTECT-010` — *Normative*

The protection layer may request bounded actions such as:

- reject an invalid command;
- force resynchronization;
- reduce trust in a prediction path;
- move a session to a stricter server-authoritative mode;
- require a fresh integrity challenge;
- disable a competitive queue while allowing ordinary/offline play;
- isolate a session for review;
- create a moderation case through Collective/provider adapters;
- terminate a session when the active game policy explicitly authorizes it.

Permanent account sanctions, cross-session restrictions, notifications, evidence retention, and appeals are service/game policy decisions, not hidden engine side effects.

### Modding, development, and accessibility compatibility `PROTECT-011` — *Normative*

Protection policy explicitly declares:

- which package roles and mod signatures are allowed;
- whether local/private servers accept unsigned content;
- whether a modded client can join unmodded or competitive sessions;
- debugger, hot-reload, console, overlay, capture, accessibility, and automation-tool rules;
- how a user can tell which compatibility mode is active;
- how a developer tests both protected and mod-friendly paths.

Accessibility software and assistive devices are not presumed hostile. Where a competitive rule must restrict a class of modification, the project must document the reason, provide the least restrictive practical path, and test real assistive workflows. Protection failures caused by Meridian bugs require recovery and support evidence, not blame shifted to the user.

### Privacy, transparency, and retention `PROTECT-012` — *Normative*

Protection collects the minimum evidence necessary for the selected game policy.

It MUST provide:

- a developer-visible inventory of collected signal classes;
- a player-facing disclosure appropriate to the game and jurisdiction;
- retention, deletion, export, access, and encryption policy for personal evidence;
- secret/redaction rules for logs and support bundles;
- separation between local diagnostics, server evidence, moderation records, and optional provider telemetry;
- no reuse of game-specific integrity evidence for unrelated Meridian purposes without a separate explicit legal/consent basis.

The engine itself does not secretly upload protection telemetry to Dead Signal Works.

### Platform and product-profile behavior `PROTECT-013` — *Normative*

- **Web:** relies primarily on server authority, package/content integrity available through web delivery, protocol validation, and semantic behavior evidence. Browser sandbox limitations are explicit.
- **Mobile:** uses qualified platform signing/attestation and user-mode checks where permitted; no JIT or privileged component is assumed.
- **Desktop:** may use stronger bounded user-mode integrity strategies, but platform support is evidence-based and compatibility failures remain typed.
- **Consoles:** platform-holder capabilities are integrated only under actual SDK/access and certification rules.
- **Dedicated servers:** do not ship client protection code; they host validation, challenge issuance, evidence correlation, and policy enforcement required by the selected profile.
- **Single-player/offline:** protection is disabled by default unless the game has a concrete local integrity requirement; DRM is not inferred.

### Diagnostics and explainability `PROTECT-014` — *Normative*

Developer diagnostics must answer:

- which profile and policy revision are active;
- which checks were included or stripped from this product;
- which platform capabilities are available, degraded, denied, or unsupported;
- why a package/module/evidence item failed validation;
- which server rule rejected a command;
- which signals contributed to a protective action;
- what alternative explanations or uncertainty remain;
- whether a mod, overlay, debugger, accessibility tool, compatibility layer, or provider adapter affected the result;
- how much CPU, memory, startup, bandwidth, storage, and latency the protection path consumed;
- how to reproduce the behavior in a safe test environment.

Public/player-facing messages remain safe and understandable without revealing bypass-sensitive detail. Internal details are capability-scoped and redacted by role.

### Failure and recovery `PROTECT-015` — *Normative*

Failure states include unavailable attestation, stale evidence, challenge timeout, provider outage, unsupported platform, clock skew, corrupt manifest, partial update, server disagreement, false-positive report, lost connectivity, denied permission, and protection-component crash.

The selected policy declares what happens for each class. A missing optional signal MUST NOT silently become evidence of cheating. Where safe, running sessions may continue in a degraded mode; competitive queues may require a retry or refuse entry without banning the player. Update rollback retains the last known-good signed release and policy.

### Zero-baggage disabled behavior `PROTECT-016` — *Normative*

A product that does not select protection MUST prove absence of protection-specific:

- runtime modules;
- background hosts;
- tasks/threads/listeners;
- telemetry endpoints;
- integrity manifests beyond general package/signing metadata;
- editor panels and settings;
- provider SDKs;
- package chunks;
- startup work;
- recurring CPU, memory, disk, network, or GPU cost.

Shared general facilities such as package hashing, secure update verification, protocol validation, and typed diagnostics remain only when the product independently uses them.

### Meridian 1.0 floor and later expansion `PROTECT-017` — *Normative*

The 1.0 floor is the balanced foundation:

- profiles and product stripping;
- server-authoritative validation hooks and generated schema checks;
- signed package/module verification;
- bounded evidence contracts;
- selected qualified user-mode integrity checks on supported desktop targets;
- mod/development compatibility modes;
- diagnostics, privacy disclosure, failure states, and provider seams.

A large proprietary detector network, global reputation system, advanced behavioral ML platform, operated moderation service, or arms-race-heavy anti-tamper program is **not** a Meridian 1.0 requirement. Such work requires a separately funded, continuously maintained, adversarial security program.

### Qualification portfolio `PROTECT-018` — *Normative*

Production qualification includes at least:

1. modified client command and impossible-state fixtures;
2. replay, duplication, reordering, stale epoch, and rate-abuse tests;
3. altered/extra/missing module and partial-update tests;
4. challenge freshness, replay, timeout, and coordinator failure tests;
5. mod-friendly and competitive profiles from the same project;
6. debugger/overlay/capture/accessibility compatibility fixtures;
