The left default dock uses tabs rather than simultaneous walls of trees:

```text
Scene | Assets | Project
```

Optional additional tabs may include Collections, Prefabs, Packages, Changes, or domain-specific sources when relevant.

##### Scene tab

- tree/hierarchy;
- search/filter;
- visibility/lock/source-state columns only when useful;
- selected object tracks viewport selection;
- unloaded/streamed content has explicit state rather than disappearing;
- stable identity survives filtering and reordering.

##### Assets tab

- list/grid/details switch;
- Collections and Smart Views;
- fast filters;
- provenance/status/usage when requested;
- "Show in source", dependencies, dependents, usage and build-inclusion explanations are one action away.

##### Project tab

- honest physical source tree;
- no fake tags pretending to be directories;
- generated/cache artifacts excluded unless explicitly requested.

#### Universal Launcher

The launcher is a centered transient surface, roughly 640–820 logical px wide depending on window size.

It opens instantly with focus in the query field.

Result anatomy:

```text
icon/type  primary title                       shortcut / status
           context / path / reason
```

Typed lanes may be shown as subtle chips or prefixes, but typing punctuation is never required.

Immediate command matches appear before slower indexed lanes finish.

The launcher can:

- execute commands;
- open documents;
- jump to entities/assets;
- change settings;
- switch workspaces;
- expose unavailable features as explicit "Enable/Add capability" actions;
- reveal active keybindings;
- show why a result is unavailable.

It is not a chatbot.

#### Drawers and transient work

Use a **bottom contextual drawer** for things users need frequently but not constantly:

- Activity;
- Problems;
- Console;
- Terminal;
- Build log;
- profiler details;
- debugger console;
- timeline where a workspace does not need it permanently.

The drawer remembers height per workspace and can be promoted into a regular dock/window.

Unlike a modal, it does not stop work.

#### Workspace designs

##### World

Default:

```text
left: Scene / Assets / Project
center: 3D viewport
right: Inspector
bottom drawer: Activity / Problems / Console
```

The viewport dominates. Contextual overlays appear near the selected object or viewport edges, not as permanent chrome.

World Environment is either a focused World sub-workspace/task surface or a dedicated curated workspace when its complexity warrants it; it must still operate on the same source.

##### 2D

Default:

```text
left: Scene / Tiles / Assets
center: 2D canvas
right: Inspector / Camera profile / layer properties
bottom: animation or tile-rule drawer when relevant
```

Pixel-perfect and continuous-coordinate modes are visible as explicit presentation profiles.

##### Code

Default:

```text
left: Project / symbols / source
center: one or more code panes
right: outline / docs / contextual inspector (optional)
bottom: Problems / Terminal / Debug / Tests
```

Code is not a second-class embedded text box. It gets a real IDE layout.

AI, when enabled, may be a normal pinnable task pane, not a mandatory right sidebar.

##### UI

Default:

```text
left: component tree / assets
center: visual .mui canvas + responsive preview
right: Inspector / style / token / state controls
bottom: Problems / states / timeline when animation is active
```

A source tab can open the same `.mui` document text. Visual and text editing mutate the same source authority.

##### Model / CAD

Default:

```text
left: feature/history tree + model browser
center: 3D model/sketch viewport
right: Inspector / constraints / feature parameters
bottom: constraints/problems/activity
```

Sketch mode visibly changes the local context strip, not the whole application identity.

History is first-class and source-linked.

##### Animate

Default:

```text
left: rig / clips / motion sources
center: character viewport
right: semantic rig / contact / layer inspector
bottom: timeline / graph / contribution map
```

The contribution debugger can explain which motion source owns each region.

##### Audio

Default:

```text
left: audio assets / buses / events
center: mixer, graph, waveform, spatial view as task requires
right: Inspector
bottom: meters / diagnostics / activity
```

Meters are visually prominent only while monitoring; inactive audio tools do not permanently animate.

##### Profile / Debug

Default:

```text
left: sessions / captures / traces
center: timeline / flame / frame / graph view
right: selection details / causality / source
bottom: diagnostics / console / raw events
```

This workspace is dense by design, but density is structured rather than cluttered.

##### Build / Release / Server

These begin as task-focused surfaces invoked from Build/launcher rather than permanent top-level workspaces in every project.

If a project's workflow uses them heavily they may be pinned as workspaces.

#### Direct manipulation and viewport overlays

Keep the permanent transform tool vocabulary tiny:

- Select;
- Move;
- Rotate;
- Scale.

Specialized handles appear only when selection/context warrants them.

Examples:

- light radius/cone;
- spline points/tangents;
- audio volume/falloff;
- physics constraints;
- NAV links;
- UI anchors/bounds;
- Artus contacts;
- Alluvium fields.

Overlay rules:

- handles are legible against bright/dark content;
- hidden/occluded handles remain predictable;
- selection uses a clean outline/tint, not a huge glowing bloom;
- snap indicators appear only while snapping;
- numeric inline entry appears close to the manipulated thing;
- cancel always restores the accepted transaction state;
- hover feedback is immediate;
- tool switching never destroys selection unexpectedly.

#### Motion

Motion exists to explain continuity, not decorate.

Target durations:

- hover/press feedback: effectively immediate, <= ~80 ms visual transition;
- small popover/menu: ~100–140 ms;
- drawer/panel reveal: ~120–180 ms;
- workspace continuity/crossfade: <= ~180 ms and never blocks input;
- toasts/status transitions: subtle;
- direct manipulation: no easing lag between pointer and object.

Rules:

- no animated background gradients;
- no bouncing toolbar icons;
- no progress animations stealing attention for ordinary background work;
- no transition may delay a command becoming usable;
- repeated rapid navigation cancels/retargets cleanly;
- Reduced Motion removes nonessential motion while preserving state clarity.

#### Icons

Use one Meridian icon family:

- mostly 16–18 logical px;
- consistent stroke/optical weight;
- filled variants only where state needs them;
- no mixture of random icon libraries;
- unfamiliar actions receive text labels or tooltips;
- destructive actions never depend on color/icon alone.

Domain icons may exist, but they should not turn the editor into a row of unexplained pictograms.

#### Empty, loading, unavailable, and error states

##### Empty state

An empty panel should answer:

1. What is this?
2. Why is it empty?
3. What is the normal next action?

Example:

```text
No animation clip selected
Select a clip or create one to edit keys and motion layers.
[Create Clip]   [Choose Existing]
```

No marketing copy.

##### Loading/background work

Prefer:

- immediate last-known-good content;
- unobtrusive progress;
- stale indicator when needed;
- cancellable Activity job.

Avoid blanking the whole workspace because an importer or compiler is running.

##### Unavailable capability

Show:

```text
Ray tracing is unavailable on this target
Reason: current WebGPU profile does not expose the required capability.
[View target requirements]
```

Do not gray out unexplained controls.

##### Error

Errors must name:

- what failed;
- what remains valid;
- affected source;
- recovery/next action;
- diagnostics/details link.

#### AI visual behavior

AI is optional and visually subordinate to the creator application.

When disabled:

- no AI button residue;
- no AI worker;
- no AI panels;
- no AI-specific index;
- no AI traces;
- no AI network activity.

When enabled:

- one task/conversation surface;
- contextual "Ask / Plan / Fix / Explain" commands where appropriate;
- provider/local/remote identity visible but not loud;
- Planning mode has an unmistakable read-only state;
- proposed changes use the same semantic diff/review UI as human changes;
- subagent/orchestration internals stay hidden until Inspector/trace view is opened;
- no sparkle iconography requirement;
- no fake avatars/personas.

#### Accessibility and scale

Visual target must survive:

- 100–400% text scaling where required by Meridian UI contracts;
- high-DPI displays;
- high-contrast mode;
- Reduced Motion;
- keyboard-only operation;
- screen-reader semantics;
- color-vision deficiencies;
- large pointer/cursor settings;
- localization expansion.

The layout should reflow/collapse before text overlaps or clips.

#### Responsiveness

At reduced width:

1. collapse optional right task panels into tabs/drawers;
2. collapse the left dock;
3. move nonessential top-bar actions into overflow;
4. preserve the primary work surface and core tool strip.

Do not simply shrink everything.

#### Multi-window

Any compatible panel/workspace may become a separate window.

A detached window:

- remains part of the same Project Session;
- shares source authority;
- has local focus/layout state;
- can contain its own top-local context strip;
- does not duplicate project services;
- recovers to the main monitor if its monitor disappears.

#### Theme and customization

Users may customize:

- dark/light/system appearance;
- accent;
- UI density;
- UI/text/code fonts and sizes;
- icon scale within supported bounds;
- workspace layouts;
- panel positions;
- keymap;
- viewport theme options.

Projects may recommend UI/layout profiles only through explicit opt-in. A repository cannot silently restyle a developer's entire Meridian application.

#### AOT acceptance tests

The editor visual target is accepted only when:

- first launch is understandable with no layout setup;
- World viewport remains visually dominant on a 1440p laptop-class screen;
- 1080p remains genuinely usable;
- 4K/high-DPI does not become microscopic;
- light and dark themes both look intentional;
- 200%+ text scaling remains operable;
- inspector/property walls remain progressively disclosed;
- launcher appears inside one interactive frame under warm conditions;
- dock resize, detach, restore, monitor loss, DPI change, and extension removal recover safely;
- screen-reader focus order matches visual task order;
- novice tests can build/run/edit without Ponder or AI;
- expert tests can expose full source/provenance/technical state;
- screenshots do not resemble a generic web dashboard;
- motion never delays interaction;
- disabled capabilities disappear instead of leaving dead chrome;
- AI-off screenshots contain no AI-specific UI.

## Detailed first-class 2D contract


### Canonical first-class 2D decisions — *Normative*


#### Continuous source/world coordinates with explicit pixel profiles `TWO-004`

Meridian 2D uses continuous subpixel-capable coordinates as the canonical authoring/runtime spatial model. Pixel-art behavior is an explicit project/camera/asset policy over that space rather than a second scene model.

A 2D project can declare a default reference grid / pixels-per-unit policy. Cameras may select Pixel Perfect, Smooth/Subpixel or custom presentation policies. Pixel-perfect profiles provide integer alignment/scaling guarantees and diagnostics; vector/high-resolution/smooth projects retain continuous precision.

#### Common tile topology portfolio `TWO-005`

First-party 2D tooling directly supports at least:

- orthogonal/rectangular;
- isometric/diamond;
- hexagonal;
- staggered/offset grids.

Topology/orientation/origin/cell transforms are explicit. The architecture permits custom/future topology adapters without forcing arbitrary graph topology into every ordinary tilemap.

#### Raster and vector/shape content are both first-class 2D sources `TWO-006`

Sprites, atlases and tiles coexist with paths, curves, fills/strokes, polygons, gradients, editable SVG-derived/vector documents and procedural shapes.

Penumbra may compile these into tessellated, cached, SDF-like, rasterized or other qualified runtime products automatically. Source semantics remain available to authoring, source control and re-editing even when the shipping representation differs.

#### High-end dedicated 2D graphics from the production start `TWO-007`

`PRODUCT-007` applies fully to 2D. Meridian's first serious production 2D renderer must not look like a lesser fallback mode.

The production target includes:

- first-class 2D materials;
- normal/height-informed lighting where used;
- point/area/shape-appropriate 2D lights;
- artist-authored occlusion;
- stable hard/soft shadow paths;
- light masks/textures;
- HDR/emissive/bloom interaction;
- rich particles/fog/effects integration;
- tile/sprite/vector lighting integration;
- automatic target-specific quality scaling and stripping.

The implementation may share GPU primitives with Penumbra 3D, but pure 2D does not secretly instantiate a 3D scene, 3D visibility world or 3D physics world.

#### Mixed 2D/3D uses explicit dimensional bridges `TWO-008`

Mixed projects share Meridian's authoring graph but cross dimensions through inspectable bridge/composition objects rather than hidden coordinate magic.

Supported concepts may include:

- 2D canvas/layer on or in a 3D world;
- 3D viewport embedded inside a 2D world/layer;
- 2D foreground/background around 3D gameplay;
- world-space UI and diegetic displays;
- explicit parallax/perspective hybrid composition;
- explicit input, camera, depth and coordinate transforms;
- deliberate Cairn 2D↔3D interaction seams where a game truly needs them.

There is no implicit conversion of 2D and 3D collision spaces or uninspectable automatic projection that changes gameplay semantics.

### Advanced first-class 2D decisions — *Normative*

#### Two natural 2D animation levels `TWO-009` — *Normative*

Meridian provides a lightweight **Sprite Animation Clip** workflow for ordinary frame/region animation and an opt-in **Artus 2D** path for skeletal/deformable/IK/constraint-heavy characters. They share timeline, event, blending, source mapping and diagnostics where semantics genuinely match, but a simple sprite animation does not instantiate conceptual rig complexity.

Sprite clips support at minimum frame/region references, variable durations, transform/parameter curves, named events/markers, hit/hurt/gameplay markers where enabled, playback modes, deterministic timing policy and source-aware preview. Artus 2D owns the richer rig/deformation path behind the already-adopted Artus authority.

#### Semantic TileSets and visual/rule layers `TWO-010` — *Normative*

Tile authoring supports both exact visual painting and higher-level semantic painting. Typed tile/cell facets may describe terrain/material class, collision/one-way policy, navigation/traversal, surface/audio semantics, lighting/occlusion, animation, weighted variants, gameplay tags, edge/corner connectivity and prefab/object spawn intent.

Auto-tiling/terrain/rule layers are derived from semantic source and remain inspectable/overrideable. Alluvium may generate the same semantic field vocabulary, avoiding a separate procedural-only tile system.

#### Loss-aware optional 2D tool interchange `TWO-011` — *Normative*

Meridian's built-in 2D tools remain sufficient on their own. Optional first-party adapters should provide source-aware import/reimport for high-value formats such as Aseprite, Tiled, LDtk, SVG and layered PSD/PSB where legally and technically practical. Preserve useful frames, tags, layers, pivots, tile/entity metadata, collision and rules where the source format exposes them. External formats do not become mandatory Meridian project authority, and write-back is promised only for adapters that independently qualify round-trip safety.

Dependency reuse follows `RESEARCH-005` and the `LEGAL-005` relicensing/intake rules: e.g. Apache/MIT parsing/atlas libraries may be used when they materially reduce work while remaining behind Meridian contracts.

#### First-party editable 2D Camera Profiles `TWO-012` — *Normative*

The low-level camera remains simple, while optional editable profiles provide common production behavior without requiring every game to rebuild it: pixel-perfect/smooth presentation, reference resolution, aspect/crop/letterbox/integer-scaling policy, smoothing/dead zones/look-ahead, target groups, bounds/room transitions, zoom, shake channels, parallax, rails, split/multi-viewport behavior and accessibility/motion limits.

Genre-specific controllers may build on these through official framework packages rather than duplicating projection/pixel policy.

#### Huge 2D worlds are author-natural and compiler-partitioned `TWO-013` — *Normative*

Creators may author a visually/logically continuous or infinite 2D world. Explicit rooms/levels/regions remain valid semantic boundaries, but developers are not expected to hand-tune runtime chunk sizes. Meridian automatically derives runtime chunks, texture/atlas pages, collision/NAV/light/occlusion products, preload halos, streaming/residency and target-specific products from project semantics and measured budgets under `PRODUCT-006`.

The editor uses working sets for huge worlds and explains why a region is resident, rebuilt, prefetched, partitioned or downgraded.

### Compact contextual 2D product surface `TWO-014` — *Normative*

Dedicated 2D does **not** create a second giant engine interface. `PRODUCT-008` applies directly:

- a normal sprite/platformer project sees sprites, layers, cameras, collision, animation, tile tools when relevant, Play/Build and ordinary properties;
- vector editing appears when vector content is selected/created;
- Artus 2D appears when rigged/deformable animation is used;
- advanced lighting/material controls appear when those systems are used;
- large-world streaming diagnostics appear when scale justifies them;
- mixed 2D/3D bridge controls appear only at explicit dimensional bridge objects/views;
- specialized internal TWO/Penumbra/Cairn terminology is not required beginner vocabulary.

A 2D project therefore benefits from a dedicated technical path **without feeling like Meridian duplicated the entire product into a 2D edition**.

### Clean-room Celeste-like C# proving project `TWO-015` — *Normative*

Meridian's flagship public 2D capability demonstration should be a **clean-room Celeste-like precision-platforming clone/fixture implemented primarily in Meridian C#**. It is deliberately demanding: the point is to prove that Meridian can create a real, responsive, polished 2D game rather than only render a tile map.

The proving workload should cover, at minimum:

```text
C# gameplay modules through normal Meridian bindings
high-refresh / low-latency action input
Cairn 2D collision, one-way platforms and moving-platform contacts
precise acceleration / deceleration / jumping / wall interaction / dash-like movement
input buffering and movement forgiveness at gameplay/controller level
pixel-perfect and smooth camera profiles
room / level transitions and checkpoints
sprite-frame animation and optional richer Artus 2D samples
semantic tile layers and collision/NAV facets
particles, trails, screen/camera shake and high-quality 2D lighting/material effects
Wavefront music/SFX and responsive event timing
MUI menus/HUD/settings
Player Preferences/Profile persistence for controls/accessibility/audio/display
progression/checkpoint save data separately from preferences
controller hot-plug/rebinding and glyph updates
replay/determinism/input-capture diagnostics
web + desktop build paths where C# target support qualifies
performance/governor and stripped 2D-only runtime evidence
```

#### Clean-source / public-content rule

Celeste itself is a behavioral/product reference, not an asset source. Public Meridian validation must use project-owned or clearly redistributable art, audio, names, rooms and text and must not imply affiliation with the Celeste developers. Publicly released Celeste source snippets may be studied only according to their actual license/provenance; the proving game should still implement its Meridian gameplay architecture independently so the workload proves Meridian rather than merely ports another engine's internals.

#### Why C# matters

This project becomes a cross-domain qualification workload for both **first-class 2D** and **Meridian C#**. C# support does not count as production-ready merely because a trivial script compiles: this platformer must exercise bindings, events, hot reload/restart behavior where supported, diagnostics, debugging, performance, source mapping, save/network-safe schemas where relevant, and one-button Play/Build through the same language-neutral Interface Schema used by other Meridian languages.

### 2D no-silent-gap coverage audit — COMPLETE FOR FIRST PASS

The post-round audit covered: coordinates/pixel policy, raster/vector source forms, grid topology, sprite/atlas pipeline, semantic tiles and auto-layers, cameras/parallax/resolution, high-end lighting/materials, particles/effects, frame and rigged animation, Cairn 2D, NAV facets, mixed-dimensional composition, external source adapters, huge-world streaming, diagnostics, accessibility, performance automation, pure-2D stripping, C# gameplay and a real precision-platforming proving workload.

The 2D product contract is complete for this specification. Remaining choices—atlas algorithms, exact vector tessellator, batch key layout, tile chunk heuristic, light/occluder representation, pixel reconstruction filters, Cairn 2D broadphase/contact algorithms, vector cache formats and adapter implementation choices—are primarily evidence/prototype decisions. A product decision may be reopened only if qualification evidence exposes a genuine contract conflict.

**The dedicated 2D product contract is complete for this specification.**

---


## Detailed input, actions, devices, prompts, and haptics contract


### Canonical input foundation — *Normative*


#### Constrained input semantics; gameplay stays out of Input `INP-001` — *Normative*

Ordinary actions remain extremely small and approachable (`Button`, `Axis1D`, `Axis2D`-class concepts). Progressive-disclosure input semantics may add press/release, hold, short/long press, tap/multi-tap, chord/modifier, dead-zone, saturation, inversion, scale, response curve, composites, context membership, and consumption/pass-through policy.

Input does **not** own coyote time, jump buffering, combo windows, cooldowns, movement forgiveness, interaction priority, animation state, or other logic that depends on simulation/game state. Those live in gameplay/controller/framework code. Meridian therefore avoids creating a second gameplay language inside the binding editor.

The default inspector should make a common binding look approximately like:

```text
Jump
  Keyboard   Space
  Gamepad    South Button

[Advanced…]
```

not like an interaction graph.

#### Small standard device vocabulary + typed capability facets `INP-002` — *Normative*

Conventional controllers expose a stable semantic vocabulary for ordinary code. Optional device capabilities are separately discoverable and typed: sensors, touch surfaces, additional paddles/buttons, richer haptics, adaptive/resistive trigger output, LEDs, battery/connection information and vendor/platform extension facets where justified.

Projects query capabilities rather than hard-code controller brands. The common abstraction is intentionally **not** expanded until every unusual device can be represented without extensions. Unknown/raw controls remain inspectable/bindable through advanced provider surfaces when safe.

#### Generated controls UI is an editable project starting point, not a permanent Meridian overlay `INP-003` — *Normative*

From a project's action schema Meridian can generate a polished MUI Controls/Input settings surface with binding capture, conflict handling, duplicate policy, reset behavior, sensitivity/dead-zone/inversion controls where declared, vibration/haptic preferences, accessibility-compatible navigation, and local-player support.

The generated surface becomes normal project-editable MUI. Projects can restyle/recompose/replace it while retaining the stable binding/profile backend. Regeneration cannot silently destroy authored edits. This avoids both repetitive per-game plumbing and the undesirable effect where every Meridian game's options menu looks like Meridian itself.

Binding/user choices persist through `SAVE-001` Player Preferences/Profile rather than progression save slots.

#### Simultaneous input with meaningful-origin prompt resolution `INP-004` — *Normative*

Compatible devices may operate simultaneously. Prompt/glyph presentation uses per-local-player **meaningful semantic activity**, with drift/noise rejection and hysteresis rather than raw last-event switching. The resolver uses actual current bindings and can surface keyboard, generic gamepad, platform-family glyphs or text labels.

Player-facing override is required (for example Automatic / Keyboard / Xbox-like / PlayStation-like / Generic / Text-only where supported). Rebinding, device reconnect and provider changes update prompt origin without project code manually swapping icon packs.

#### Broad device architecture, selective qualification `INP-005` — *Normative*

The production architecture directly accommodates keyboard, mouse/high-resolution pointer, text/IME, standard gamepads, multi-touch/basic gestures, pen/stylus, mobile motion where useful, and modern controller sensors/touch/haptics through capabilities.

Wheels, pedals, HOTAS/flight sticks, arcade/specialized controllers, accessibility hardware and unusual HID classes use the same device/action/provider architecture but are qualified device families only when Meridian has hardware/test evidence. 1.0 does **not** promise polished first-party support for every peripheral category. XR tracked poses/controllers stay in XR while interoperating with shared action concepts.

`PRODUCT-008` applies directly: unused specialist-device UI/providers must remain invisible/stripped from ordinary projects.

### Cross-system consequences — *Normative*

- `SAVE-001` owns durable per-game player preferences/bindings; Input owns schemas/validation and active resolved maps.
- MUI owns controls/prompt presentation; Input publishes semantic binding/glyph/capability data.
- CORE owns device identity, normalization and local-player assignment; gameplay frameworks consume semantic actions.
- Replay records semantic input plus the relevant resolved mapping/configuration identity, never transient OS handles.
- Steam Input, SDL3, gilrs, platform-native APIs and future providers are adapters behind Meridian contracts; no provider-specific public type becomes authoritative.
- The clean-room Celeste-like C# proving project `TWO-015` must validate keyboard and controller rebinding, prompt switching, low-latency action delivery and preferences persistence from C# rather than relying on Rust-only privileged paths.

### Research-informed implementation notes

#### Context layering
Steam Input's action-set layers demonstrate the usefulness of a base context plus small overlays, while its own documentation warns that excessive layers confuse players. Meridian should therefore support contextual layering but keep the normal model bounded and inspectable rather than exposing arbitrary stack gymnastics as an everyday feature.

#### Sensors and output capabilities
Current SDL3 exposes standardized gamepad semantics plus sensor and haptic APIs. The W3C Gamepad specification exposes a low-level gamepad model and a primary haptic actuator for web-capable devices. These reinforce `INP-002`: device output/sensors need capability negotiation and graceful fallback, not brand tests.

#### Provider candidates and licensing
SDL3 is zlib-licensed and remains a serious cross-platform provider candidate/reference. `gilrs` is MIT/Apache-2.0 and currently provides normalized gamepad layout, mappings, hotplug/reconnect, rumble and power information. Both preserve Meridian-owned licensing under `RESEARCH-005`/`LEGAL-005`; the provider decision remains evidence-based because platform coverage, native-feature depth, web behavior, maintenance and latency differ.

### Advanced input decisions — *Normative*


#### One primary action context plus a bounded ordered overlay set `INP-006` — *Normative*

Each `LocalPlayerId` has at most one primary action context at a time (`Gameplay`, `Menu`, `Vehicle`, `Spectator`, project-defined equivalents) and zero or more narrowly scoped overlays (`Aiming`, `RadialMenu`, temporary photo-mode modifier, etc.). The public product does not encourage arbitrary context graphs.

Required semantics:

- the primary context provides the default visible action vocabulary for that player;
- overlays declare explicit order/priority;
- an overlay may add an action, alter a binding interpretation, consume an action, or pass it through;
- an action resolution trace records the primary context, every considered overlay, the winning binding, and the reason an event was consumed or ignored;
- deep/ambiguous stacks produce an editor warning and profiler/debug trace rather than silently becoming normal architecture;
- context changes are typed transactions at defined input synchronization points;
- context transitions never mutate already-published immutable tick snapshots;
- UI focus contexts and gameplay contexts are coordinated but not conflated: MUI owns focus semantics while Input owns action routing;
- overlay state is not a hidden gameplay state machine. Gameplay decides **when** an overlay is requested; Input decides how actions resolve while it is active.

Anti-bloat consequence: ordinary projects can live entirely with `Gameplay` + `Menu`. The editor does not show a context-stack designer until the project creates additional contexts.

#### Portable player binding profile plus optional device-local calibration/overrides `INP-007` — *Normative*

Durable player binding intent is expressed against semantic controls or device classes where possible rather than ephemeral OS handles or one physical controller serial number.

Conceptual persistence split:

```text
Player Preferences/Profile
  action bindings
  prompt/glyph preference
  sensitivity/inversion intent
  vibration/haptic preference
  accessibility-related input choices

Device-local input overlay
  physical-device identity where safe/useful
  stick calibration
  dead-zone correction
  gyro calibration
  trigger calibration
  device-only paddle/extension mapping
  provider-specific capability state
```

Rules:

1. Replacing a conventional gamepad should normally preserve the player's gameplay bindings.
2. Device-specific special bindings are preserved when their device is absent and become `Unavailable`, not silently deleted.
3. A provider may resolve a portable semantic control to a device-specific physical control, but provider-local IDs do not become canonical persistence authority.
4. Machine-specific calibration is not blindly cloud-synced to another machine/device.
5. Binding migration is schema-versioned and inspectable.
6. Conflicting imported/cloud bindings require deterministic conflict policy and visible user resolution when automatic safe reconciliation is impossible.
7. Projects can declare multiple binding presets without forcing users to understand physical input APIs.

#### Optional first-party Player Join / local assignment service `INP-008` — *Normative*

CORE remains authority for device identity and typed assignment transactions. Meridian additionally provides a small optional first-party join pattern so local-multiplayer games do not have to rebuild device-assignment plumbing.

Conceptual flow:

```text
unassigned meaningful input
-> project-declared Join eligibility
-> select/create LocalPlayerId
-> associate DeviceAssignment
-> load Player Preferences/Profile
-> resolve ActionMap + contexts
-> assign viewport/UI focus/audio listener policy
-> publish committed PlayerContext
```

Required behavior:

- touching an unassigned controller does **not** automatically spawn a player unless the project explicitly selects that behavior;
- "Press any button to join" is a framework/editor convenience over the typed assignment service, not a CORE hard-coded rule;
- reconnect can reclaim a previous player slot by declared policy;
- keyboard/mouse sharing, paired controllers, one device controlling multiple roles, and device transfer between players require explicit project policy;
- assignment conflicts are presented in customizable MUI and leave prior valid ownership intact until a transaction commits;
- dedicated/headless/server profiles do not instantiate local-device join infrastructure;
- local player identity is independent from optional Collective/online account identity, though an explicit association may exist.

#### One canonical timestamped input stream with purpose-specific immutable views `INP-009` — *Normative*

Meridian captures platform/device events as early as practical, normalizes them once through the owning input path, and derives multiple safe views instead of allowing subsystems to poll hardware independently.

Authoritative model:

```text
platform/device event
-> timestamp + device identity
-> provider normalization
-> canonical input event stream
-> binding/action resolution
   -> fixed-tick authoritative InputSnapshot
   -> latest presentation state
   -> bounded edge/event view for explicitly eligible latency-sensitive consumers
-> trace correlation to simulation and presented frame
```

Hard rules:

- authoritative gameplay/replay/network simulation consumes the fixed-tick snapshot or another explicitly declared deterministic input contract;
- UI/cursor/presentation may consume a newer presentation view without changing authoritative simulation state;
- the same physical event cannot accidentally perform the same gameplay mutation through two views;
- no renderer, gameplay framework, MUI control, plugin, or provider may bypass Input ownership and directly poll a controller for authoritative game actions;
- platform-specific low-latency APIs are implementation strategies behind the same contract;
- event timestamps preserve enough provenance to measure input-to-simulation and input-to-present latency;
- catch-up simulation cannot invent intermediate raw input events;
- replay carries the semantic input stream plus configuration/binding identity required to reproduce declared deterministic behavior.

Performance obligation:

Meridian must expose at minimum:

```text
OS/provider event timestamp
normalized-event timestamp
action-resolution timestamp
assigned fixed tick
simulation-consumption timestamp
presented-frame identifier/time where measurable
```

The latency profiler should show distributions and worst cases, not only one average.

#### Small semantic haptic/feedback layer plus advanced capability facets `INP-010` — *Normative*

Ordinary haptic authoring is deliberately small:

```text
HapticClip / FeedbackEvent
  duration
  amplitude/intensity
  optional envelope
  optional channel/semantic intent
  interruption/mix policy
```

Advanced device outputs (multi-actuator hardware, adaptive/resistive triggers, HD haptics, LEDs where treated as feedback, etc.) are optional typed capability facets.

Rules:

- one simple feedback event must degrade to ordinary rumble or no output without gameplay breakage;
- per-player vibration enabled/intensity/accessibility choices come from Player Preferences/Profile;
- unsupported required advanced output is a typed capability failure or explicit fallback, never silent brand guessing;
- haptic effects have bounded lifetime and cancellation; disconnect cannot leave a device in a stuck feedback state;
- feedback does not become an audio/DSP-style graph system in core Input;
- Wavefront may provide timing/audio-derived triggers through typed events, but Input/device output remains owner of controller actuators;
- provider-specific actuator handles never enter game save data.

### Canonical Input architecture — *Normative*

The following contract defines Meridian Input authority, semantics, runtime behavior, and qualification requirements.

#### Product promise

Input should feel almost trivial for the common case and still scale to unusual devices:

```text
Create action "Jump"
bind Space + Gamepad South
use action in gameplay
```

A developer should not need to understand SDL mappings, HID usages, platform handles, controller databases, polling frequency, IME composition, local-player assignment graphs, or haptic actuator formats to ship a normal keyboard/mouse/controller game.

Advanced capability appears only when the project asks for it.

#### Authority map

| Concern | Authority | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| platform raw events | platform adapter | untrusted, timestamped, device-scoped input |
| normalized device/control identity | Input/CORE | provider-specific details retained as provenance |
| device capabilities | Input provider contract | semantic standard controls + optional capability facets |
| action schema and bindings | Input | project-declared semantic actions |
| active primary context/overlays | Input | gameplay requests context changes; Input resolves actions |
| MUI focus/text/IME widgets | MUI + platform text service | key actions cannot substitute for text composition |
| device -> local player assignment | CORE Input | typed committed transactions |
| gameplay meaning of actions | gameplay/framework | Input never owns jump/coyote/combo/game rules |
| durable binding preference | Player Preferences/Profile | `SAVE-001` |
| device-local calibration | local device settings overlay | not blindly portable/cloud-synced |
| controller glyph visual assets | MUI/asset system | Input provides semantic origin/glyph key |
| haptic actuator output | Input/provider | project emits semantic feedback intent |
| replay/network input identity | Input + replay/network | semantic snapshots plus config hash/provenance |
| XR tracked poses | XR | may share actions; fixed pose semantics remain XR-owned |

#### Semantic contracts

Exact Rust, C#, and IR spelling remains implementation work, but implementations MUST preserve concepts equivalent to:

```text
InputDeviceId
InputProviderId
ControlId
ActionId
ActionMapId
ActionContextId
LocalPlayerId
BindingProfileId
DeviceCalibrationId
HapticClipId

InputDeviceDescriptor {
  stable_runtime_identity,
  provider,
  device_class,
  semantic_layout,
  capabilities,
  connection,
  power_state?,
  provenance
}

InputEvent {
  event_id,
  monotonic_timestamp,
  device,
  control,
  kind,
  raw_or_normalized_value,
  provider_sequence,
  provenance
}

ActionDefinition {
  id,
  value_type: Button | Axis1D | Axis2D,
  interactions?,
  processors?,
  contexts,
  consumption_policy,
  accessibility_metadata,
  display_metadata
}

Binding {
  action,
  device_class_or_capability,
  control_or_composite,
  modifiers,
  optional_provider_extension,
  conflict_policy
}

InputSnapshot {
  tick,
  configuration_hash,
  local_player,
  resolved_actions,
  context_revision,
  binding_revision,
  source_event_range
}

ActionResolutionTrace {
  event,
  candidate_bindings,
  contexts,
  overlays,
  processors,
  winner,
  consumption_reason,
  resulting_action
}
```

#### Interaction/processor ceiling

Allowed built-in input-level semantics include:

- press / release;
- hold and bounded duration threshold;
- short/long press when defined solely by input timing;
- tap / bounded multi-tap;
- chord / modifier;
- dead zone / anti-dead-zone only if evidence justifies anti-dead-zone;
- saturation;
- axis scale/invert;
- response curve;
- digital-to-axis composites;
- radial/axial dead-zone strategy;
- consumption/pass-through;
- device-class filtering.

Not Input:

- coyote time;
- jump buffer tied to grounded state;
- combo rules;
- cooldowns;
- animation transitions;
- action eligibility from inventory/physics/state machine;
- aim assist;
- movement smoothing that changes gameplay semantics;
- camera behavior beyond raw action output.

#### Editor UX

Default Input workspace should expose only:

```text
Actions
  Move       Axis2D
  Jump       Button
  Interact   Button

Bindings
  Move       WASD / Left Stick
  Jump       Space / South
  Interact   E / West

[Test Inputs]
[Generate Controls UI]
[Advanced…]
```

Advanced surfaces may expose:

- interaction/processor chains;
- context/overlay resolution;
- local-player assignment;
- provider/device capabilities;
- raw event monitor;
- calibration;
- glyph mapping;
- replay/config hashes;
- haptic test surface;
- latency trace.

No unused specialist device categories should crowd the normal inspector.

#### Generated Controls UI contract

Generated project UI is a **starting artifact**, not runtime engine chrome.

It should be able to include only relevant controls:

- bindings by input class;
- sensitivity/inversion when project actions expose them;
- vibration/haptic settings if project uses feedback;
- prompt style if multiple glyph families exist;
- per-local-player selection where the game supports it;
- reset to project defaults;
- conflict resolution;
- accessibility-related input preferences selected by project/engine policy.

Regeneration rules must distinguish generated-owned regions from human-authored edits. No generator may destroy customized project UI silently.

#### Threading and timing

- platform callbacks/adapters may collect events on platform-owned threads but must transfer through bounded queues/contracts;
- no unbounded allocation or lock contention on latency-critical input collection paths;
- fixed-tick snapshots publish atomically at simulation barriers;
- haptic output is scheduled/cancelled without blocking gameplay simulation;
- device enumeration/hotplug may run asynchronously but assignment changes commit transactionally;
- text/IME composition follows platform/UI requirements and is not delayed to fixed gameplay ticks;
- background device database updates cannot change an active mapping mid-tick without a revision transition.

#### Persistence and cloud boundaries

Portable player preferences:

- action bindings;
- preferred glyph family/automatic mode;
- sensitivity/invert preferences;
- vibration/haptic preference;
- accessibility input choices;
- project-defined input preferences.

Device-local data:

- physical calibration;
- device-specific drift compensation;
- provider-specific calibration cache;
- ephemeral OS handles;
- transport state;
- battery/connection state.

Cloud sync must never merge device-local calibration into an unrelated device merely because a profile shares a user account.

#### Failure and recovery behavior

Required explicit cases:

- device disconnect during held action -> release/cancel according to declared policy, never sticky input;
- provider crash/failure -> last state invalidated, safe neutral state published, actionable diagnostic;
- mapping database missing/stale -> generic/raw fallback where safe plus visible degraded capability;
- ambiguous controller identity after reconnect -> do not silently steal another player's assignment;
- binding references unavailable control -> preserve preference and mark unresolved;
- deep/ambiguous context stack -> warning + trace; no random priority;
- haptic failure -> gameplay continues unless project explicitly required exact feedback capability;
- focus loss -> clear/transition pressed state according to deterministic platform policy;
- IME/text focus -> gameplay consumption rules must prevent accidental action leakage where UI declares exclusive text focus;
- replay config mismatch -> typed mismatch rather than pretending deterministic equivalence.

#### Diagnostics

Input diagnostics should answer:

- What physical/provider event happened?
- Which device and local player owned it?
- Which action(s) were candidates?
- Which context/overlay won?
- Which processor changed the value?
- Why was it consumed/ignored?
- What binding revision was active?
- Which fixed tick consumed it?
- Which presented frame first reflected it?
- Why did the prompt glyph change?
- Why did a device fail to join/reconnect?
- Which fallback mapped a haptic request?

Required views include a compact live Input Inspector, raw/normalized event trace, action-resolution trace, assignment map, capability view, binding conflict view, and latency timeline.

#### Performance and optimization obligations

Input is a foundational hot path and must remain cheap even when advanced features exist.

- Common keyboard/mouse/controller action resolution should be allocation-free or effectively allocation-free per event/frame after setup.
- Bindings and context tables should be compiled/indexed rather than linearly scanning arbitrary project objects each event.
- Glyph resolution and settings UI metadata must not run on the action hot path.
- Raw event history is bounded; diagnostic capture can raise retention explicitly.
- Capability providers load only when platform/project needs them.
- Haptic output queues are bounded and coalesce/replace where policy allows.
- Latency measurements must distinguish collection latency, action-routing latency, simulation wait, and render/present delay.
- 2D/Celeste-like validation requires high-refresh input behavior; the engine should not assume 60 Hz rendering merely because simulation has a fixed step.

#### Dependency strategy

Candidate roles, not frozen selections:

| Candidate | License posture | Candidate role | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|
| SDL3 | zlib | broad native input/device backend; controller DB/sensors/haptics | benchmark platform coverage, latency, native-feature access |
| gilrs | MIT OR Apache-2.0 | Rust-native gamepad provider/reference | compare mappings/hotplug/rumble/power/platform gaps |
| Steam Input | Steamworks platform SDK | optional Steam provider/adapter | provider-neutral actions/glyphs; no Steam-only public API |
| web Gamepad/Pointer APIs | web standards/browser | web provider | browser capability and permission/fallback tests |
| platform-native APIs | platform SDK | advanced native provider facets | only when generic provider cannot expose required capability |

Meridian may use mature dependencies when they materially help and remain compatible with `RESEARCH-005`/`RESEARCH-007` and `LEGAL-005`. Reimplementing mappings/haptics merely to avoid a permissible dependency is not a product goal.

#### Validation/evidence gates

At minimum:

1. keyboard + mouse + standard controller complete game flow;
2. rebinding conflict and recovery fixture;
3. device disconnect/reconnect while buttons are held;
4. two-to-four local players joining/leaving/reassigning;
5. keyboard/mouse + controller simultaneous use with stable prompt switching;
6. stick-drift/noise fixture proving glyph hysteresis;
7. text/IME focus without gameplay leakage;
8. replay of semantic inputs with configuration-hash match/mismatch tests;
9. fixed-tick plus high-refresh presentation latency trace;
10. simple rumble fallback and unsupported-advanced-haptic behavior;
11. device-local calibration not leaking to another device/profile;
12. stripped keyboard/mouse-only and headless builds proving unused providers/haptics do not remain;
13. C# proving project exercises the same public Input surface as Rust gameplay;
14. accessibility/navigation validation of generated Controls UI.


## Detailed save, persistence, profile, migration, and recovery contract

### Per-game Player Preferences/Profile is separate from gameplay saves `SAVE-001` — *Normative*

Meridian games have a first-class **Player Preferences/Profile** persistence layer that is distinct from ordinary progression/world save slots.

The minimum conceptual separation is:

```text
Game runtime persistence
├── Player Preferences / Profile
│   ├── controls and rebinding
│   ├── accessibility
│   ├── audio
│   ├── display / presentation
│   ├── language / locale
│   ├── comfort / camera preferences
│   └── project-defined typed preference fields
│
├── Progression / Save Slots
│   ├── campaign / character / run progression
│   ├── checkpoints
│   └── project-defined gameplay state
│
├── World / Persistent Region State
│   └── large or streamed semantic patches where the game uses them
│
└── Session / transient state
    └── never treated as durable preference/progression authority
```

This prevents common user settings from being duplicated into every slot, lost when a player starts a new game, or coupled to one particular world save.

**Canonical policy:**

- Player Preferences/Profile exists even when the game has no progression save system.
- Preference data uses typed schemas, versioning, migration, validation, unknown-field preservation, and bounded recovery rather than an untyped arbitrary blob.
- A project may extend the preference schema with namespaced game-specific user choices.
- World/progression state does not silently leak into preferences merely because it is convenient.
- Preferences can be reset, exported, imported, and repaired independently of save slots.
- Player-wide intent, local-user identity, device-local overlays, cloud-synced preferences, and per-controller/local-player bindings remain distinct layers with explicit merge/conflict rules.
- Device-specific display, graphics calibration, audio routing, input calibration, and hardware bindings stay device-local unless a project explicitly defines a safe portable representation.
- Accessibility and language preferences are durable user intent and do not disappear with a save-slot reset.
- Cosmetic/unlock state belongs to Profile only when the game declares it user-wide rather than progression-authoritative.
- Multiplayer/server-authoritative gameplay data is never trusted merely because a local preference document contains a similarly named field.
- Cloud/provider synchronization is optional, offline-first, conflict-visible, and never the sole copy of accepted local preferences.


### Small semantic persistence-scope model `SAVE-002` — *Normative*

Meridian defines a **small semantic persistence scope vocabulary** because different durable state classes have materially different lifetime, migration, reset, roaming, privacy, and conflict semantics. The scope model is deliberately small and progressively exposed:

```text
Device-local Settings
Player Preferences / Profile
Global Player Progression
Save Slot / World State
Session State
```

The scope names describe persistence semantics, not mandatory files, editor panels, or runtime services.

#### Device-local Settings

Examples:

- selected display/GPU/monitor;
- machine-specific graphics choices where roaming would be harmful;
- hardware calibration;
- controller-specific calibration data;
- local cache/storage preferences;
- platform-local compatibility workarounds.

Device-local settings normally **do not roam** to other machines unless a field explicitly opts into roaming and proves that it has portable meaning.

#### Player Preferences / Profile

This extends `SAVE-001`. Examples:

- input bindings;
- accessibility preferences;
- audio levels and dynamic-range preference;
- language;
- subtitle/caption presentation;
- camera comfort/motion preferences;
- vibration/haptic preference;
- project-defined player preferences that should survive starting or deleting a campaign.

A player's preferences/profile is not implicitly tied to one campaign/save slot.

#### Global Player Progression

Optional project-defined state that belongs to the player's experience of the game rather than one particular campaign/world. Examples may include:

- unlocked chapters/modes;
- meta-progression;
- discovered extras;
- aggregate statistics;
- project-defined achievement mirrors or accessibility unlocks.

Meridian does **not** assume this is an online account and does not require Collective or cloud connectivity.

#### Save Slot / World State

The durable gameplay state for a particular journey, world, run, character, campaign, simulation, etc.

The word "slot" is a UX model, not a requirement. A game can have:

- no slots;
- one journey;
- several human-visible slots;
- a custom world/save browser;
- a large persistent world without a classic slot UI.

#### Session State

Transient current-session state. It is not durable merely because it exists in memory. Promotion into another persistence scope must be explicit.

#### Anti-bloat consequence

A tiny game **does not receive five persistence panels**. If it only uses preferences and one save record, the editor and generated UI show only those concepts. The semantic vocabulary exists so Meridian can provide correct behavior when needed without requiring every project to learn it up front.

### Typed language-neutral persistence schemas `SAVE-003` — *Normative*

Meridian's canonical persistence model is **not arbitrary live-object dumping**.

Game languages get ergonomic declarations/derives/attributes that lower into a Meridian-owned language-neutral persistence schema.

Conceptual C# source:

```csharp
[Persistent("player.progress", Version = 3)]
public sealed class PlayerProgress
{
    public StableId Checkpoint { get; set; }
    public int Collectibles { get; set; }
}
```

Conceptual Rust source:

```rust
#[derive(MeridianPersistent)]
#[meridian(schema = "player.progress", version = 3)]
struct PlayerProgress {
    checkpoint: StableId,
    collectibles: u32,
}
```

Equivalent first-party bindings are expected for other supported gameplay languages when those language integrations mature.

The canonical schema records enough stable meaning for:

- schema/type identity;
- stable field identity;
- value type;
- required/optional status;
- defaults;
- schema version;
- constraints/validation;
- migration steps;
- persistence scope;
- merge/roaming policy where applicable;
- privacy/sensitivity classification where applicable.

Runtime objects/components **export to and import from** persistence records. Their process-local object address, ECS entity handle, VM identity, reflection-table slot, C# runtime type handle, Rust memory layout, or third-party solver object is never the durable format authority.

#### Convenience target

Schema-first must not mean boilerplate-first. Ordinary saveable data should be as easy to declare as safe automatic serialization systems, while preserving a durable contract Meridian can migrate and inspect.

#### Escape hatch

Projects can provide custom serializers/migrations for unusual data. Custom bytes remain wrapped in versioned Meridian records with declared bounds, owner, provenance, migration policy, and failure behavior rather than becoming invisible filesystem blobs.

### Optional Save Profile and generated editable save UI `SAVE-004` — *Normative*

Meridian provides a **small optional Save Profile** that removes routine save-system plumbing without imposing one genre's slot model.

Conceptual authoring surface:

```text
Save Model
  No Slots
  Single Journey
  Multiple Slots
  Custom

Autosave
  Off
  Checkpoints
  Periodic When Safe
  Project Events

Recovery
  Automatic
```

Meridian can provide reusable infrastructure for:

- stable slot/world identities;
- slot metadata;
- safe transaction/checkpoint scheduling;
- `Continue` resolution;
- New/Load/Delete mechanics;
- autosave event plumbing;
- optional screenshot/summary hooks;
- recovery integration;
- migration awareness;
- platform/cloud adapter integration;
- generated **editable MUI** starting interfaces.

Generated MUI is ordinary editable project UI, not a permanent engine-owned visual skin. Regeneration cannot silently destroy manual authoring.

#### Safe-point authority

Meridian does **not** decide that any arbitrary frame is semantically safe to persist. A project must either:

1. publish semantic checkpoint/save-safe events; or
2. declare and prove a save-anywhere model whose captured state is complete and restorable.

The engine owns atomic persistence machinery. The game owns the gameplay meaning of a safe checkpoint.

### Local-first, provider-neutral, scope-aware cloud synchronization `SAVE-005` — *Normative*

Local persistence is complete without an account or network.

Optional cloud/platform providers synchronize Meridian persistence documents/transactions through a provider-neutral seam. The provider is not the canonical save format.

#### Merge policy

Meridian never assumes arbitrary state is mergeable.

Default policy by scope:

```text
Device-local Settings
-> remain local unless specifically roamable

Player Preferences / Profile
-> field-level merge only where field/schema policy proves independence

Global Player Progression
-> project-declared merge operators may be used when semantics are safe
   (for example set-union or monotonic-max)

Save Slot / World State
-> divergent valid revisions remain distinct by default
-> no invented whole-world merge
```

If two save/world revisions diverge and no explicit merge contract exists, Meridian preserves both and asks the provider or user to resolve the branch.

#### Conflict metadata

A conflict record should retain enough information for a clear decision without requiring the player to understand synchronization internals:

- revision identity;
- source device/provider;
- last valid commit time;
- semantic save/world label;
- playtime/checkpoint/summary where project-supplied;
- schema/build compatibility;
- integrity status;
- whether a safe merge exists.

Platform-native conflict UX may be used where appropriate. Meridian retains a provider-neutral fallback.

### Rich bounded recovery, quiet normal UX `SAVE-006` — *Normative*

Meridian keeps strong journal/snapshot/recovery machinery underneath a simple player experience.

Normal player UX remains approximately:

```text
Continue
Load Game
New Game
```

Recovery detail is surfaced only when necessary or explicitly requested.

Example failure UX:

```text
The newest save did not finish writing.
Meridian recovered a valid save from 4:31 PM.

[Continue]
[Other Recovery Points…]
```

Developer/QA expert tooling may expose:

- journal records;
- snapshots;
- rotating recovery heads;
- checksums;
- schema versions;
- migration chain;
- repair events;
- unknown preserved records;
- source/build/plugin dependencies;
- conflict revisions;
- exact failure reason.

Recovery history is bounded by project/platform policy. Meridian does not accumulate an unbounded hidden history forever.

### Save authority matrix

| Concern | Owner | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| save envelope, journal, snapshots | `meridian-save` | game-neutral persistence mechanics |
| schema registry/migrations | Meridian persistence/schema services | language-neutral durable contracts |
| gameplay meaning of a checkpoint | game/framework | engine cannot infer semantic safety |
| Player Preferences/Profile | persistence layer + project schema | independent from campaign slots |
| device calibration | Input/platform + Device-local persistence | normally not cloud-roamed |
| cloud provider transport | platform/provider adapter | never canonical persistence authority |
| conflict semantics | schema/project + Meridian conflict engine | no arbitrary world auto-merge |
| player-facing save UI | game MUI, optionally generated | editable, replaceable presentation |
| recovery/integrity | `meridian-save` | bounded, inspectable, crash-safe |
| online identity association | Collective/provider where enabled | optional; not required for local saves |

### Save failure invariants

Meridian must not:

- erase player preferences when a campaign is deleted;
- roam machine-specific settings by default;
- serialize raw runtime handles as durable identity;
- silently skip a complete corrupt committed record and pretend the save is sound;
- silently overwrite a divergent cloud/local world revision;
- auto-merge arbitrary gameplay state without a declared safe merge contract;
- expose journal implementation terminology in normal player workflows;
- require network/account presence for local persistence;
- make generated save UI visually mandatory;
- let a language/runtime refactor silently redefine persistent field identity.

### Save evidence consequences

Later validation must include at least:

1. deleting one campaign leaves profile/preferences intact;
2. rebinding controls persists across creating/deleting save slots;
3. device-local calibration does not incorrectly roam in a provider test;
4. C# and Rust declarations lower to compatible schema semantics;
5. field/type rename migration with stable identity;
6. removed optional field migration;
7. missing required migration refuses unsafe load with recovery options;
8. interrupted write recovers previous committed head;
9. complete checksum-corrupt committed record is diagnosed rather than skipped;
10. preferences conflict safely field-merges only when declared;
11. two divergent world saves remain separate and neither is silently destroyed;
12. generated save UI can be heavily restyled/restructured without changing persistence semantics;
13. no-network/offline path passes with zero cloud/provider startup requirement;
14. tiny-project UX exposes only used persistence concepts.

The Save and Persistence product contract is complete for this specification. Huge-world persistence, migration/missing-content behavior, mods/DLC dependencies, privacy/tamper/encryption, and player/account/export portability are defined below; exact storage algorithms and thresholds remain implementation evidence.

---

### Save and persistence derived closure `SAVE-DER-001..005` — *Derived normative contract*

The remaining inventory is implementation and evidence work. The existing Save, Basalt, mod/package, Input and local-first contracts resolve the product behavior; exact storage algorithms remain engineering evidence.

#### Streamed/huge-world persistence uses semantic incremental state, not giant whole-world rewrites `SAVE-DER-001` — *Derived normative contract*

**Controlling authority:** `SAVE-003`, `SAVE-004`, `SAVE-006`, Basalt layered persistent-world patching/stable region identity and bounded journal/snapshot recovery.

Meridian persists changed semantic regions/entities/components through bounded transactions/journal records and compacts them into checkpoints/snapshots according to project/platform policy. Streaming residency is **not** save authority: unloaded regions can still have durable state. A save operation does not require every world cell resident in memory.

Exact region-index structures, compaction thresholds, snapshot cadence and compression are `PROTOTYPE` decisions.

#### Version migration is explicit, typed and recoverable `SAVE-DER-002` — *Derived normative contract*

**Controlling authority:** `SAVE-003` typed/versioned language-neutral schemas, existing migration chains, stable IDs/source authority and `SAVE-006` recovery.

- additive unknown optional data is preserved/round-tripped where the schema allows;
- known version changes run explicit migrations with diagnostics/provenance;
- missing required migration/type/semantic authority does **not** silently zero fields or fabricate success;
- the original save remains preserved and opens through inspection/recovery/migration tooling;
- engine implementation types never become persistence compatibility simply because a language/runtime changed.

Migration graph representation and optimized bulk migration are `PROTOTYPE` work.

#### Missing DLC/mod/content never triggers a destructive fake load `SAVE-DER-003` — *Derived normative contract*

**Controlling authority:** `SAVE-003`, `SAVE-006`, package/mod exact-set metadata, original MOD spec unknown-record preservation and stateful-mod migration/data-loss preview.

If missing content is declared optional and the save schema defines a safe absent behavior, Meridian may load degraded state while retaining unknown records for later restoration. If required authoritative content/type semantics are missing, Meridian preserves the save and reports the exact dependency instead of silently deleting state. Stateful mod removal requires migration, archival or an explicit data-loss preview.

#### Ordinary saves are not secret stores or magical anti-cheat cryptography `SAVE-DER-004` — *Derived normative contract*

**Controlling authority:** local-first/readable/recoverable source philosophy, `SAVE-002` scopes, `PROTECT-001`/`PROTECT-002` user-mode protection policy, server-authority/security boundaries and secret-redaction rules.

- provider credentials/signing keys/server secrets do not belong in ordinary game-save records;
- checksums/hashes/journals protect integrity/recovery but are not advertised as cheating prevention;
- optional encryption/signing may be used for platform/privacy/product requirements, but encryption-at-rest is not the default universal save format merely to obscure player-owned local data;
- privacy-sensitive fields declare purpose/retention/export behavior rather than hiding inside opaque blobs;
- competitive integrity is primarily server-authoritative where applicable.

Exact cryptographic construction is `SECURITY / RESEARCH` work and must be selected by threat-model and implementation evidence.

#### Player/profile portability remains provider-neutral `SAVE-DER-005` — *Derived normative contract*

**Controlling authority:** `SAVE-002`, `SAVE-005`, `INP-008`, provider-neutral platform services and optional Collective identity.

- `LocalPlayerId` / local player-profile ownership does not require a network account;
- explicit provider/account association may synchronize eligible scopes but does not redefine local source authority;
- device-specific settings/calibration remain local unless a field explicitly has portable meaning;
- Save Slot/World and portable Player Preferences/Profile data have first-class inspect/export/import paths where platform policy permits;
- cloud providers synchronize declared documents/scopes; they do not become the canonical data model.

**Architecture status:** The Save, Persistence, and Player Preferences product contract is complete for this specification. Corruption, migration, cloud/provider, browser, and multi-profile behavior still require implementation and qualification evidence.


## Detailed project, directory, source-projection, and build-surface contract


### Canonical project model

#### Tiny project root, flexible contents `PRJ-001` — *Normative*

A normal Meridian game project has a deliberately small set of first-party root concepts. The engine's subsystem topology must never become the game's filesystem topology. The default conceptual shape remains:

```text
MyGame/
├── project.meridian
├── Content/
├── Code/              # omitted when no authored code exists
└── .meridian/         # local/derived/recovery state; not source authority by default
```

Templates may create useful project-owned children, but no template may create dozens of empty subsystem/type directories merely because Meridian supports those capabilities.

#### Project-owned content organization `PRJ-002` — *Normative*

`Content/` is organized around the game, not mandatory asset-type buckets. The Asset Catalog supplies independent type/tag/dependency/usage/search views. Physical organization remains understandable in Finder, Explorer, terminals, source control, and third-party tools.

#### One derived-state boundary `PRJ-003` — *Normative*

Disposable generated state, toolchain intermediates, indexes, generated bindings, import products, shader/build caches, recovery data, and logs should be redirected or represented beneath the Meridian derived-state boundary and/or the shared content-addressed cache. Portable source configuration is not hidden merely because Meridian owns it.

`.meridian/` must have explicit retention and authority classes. A future clean operation must distinguish safely reconstructable data from recovery data, expensive-but-reconstructable data, user-local configuration, and anything that requires confirmation before removal.

#### Simple ordinary Play, Build, and Release workflow `PRJ-004` — *Normative*

The ordinary user is not exposed to the full internal resolve/compile/import/cook/optimize/strip/stage/package/sign/verify graph.

Meridian presents four stable intent-level actions:

- **Play** — run the selected development product with the fastest safe incremental path, preserving last-known-good behavior when a new compile/import fails.
- **Test** — execute the selected unit, integration, simulation, rendering, networking, package, or project journey under a reproducible profile.
- **Build** — create and verify a runnable local artifact for one or more selected product projections and targets. Build does not publish anything.
- **Release** — create an immutable versioned release candidate, run the required qualification/signing/notarization/provider staging graph, and optionally hand the verified artifacts to explicitly selected distribution adapters. Publishing remains a separately authorized action inside Release.

`Export` remains a domain-specific verb for assets, captures, interchange, reports, and other non-product outputs. `Package` remains an inspectable build stage and advanced command, not a competing everyday synonym for releasing a game.

Pressing Play/Build/Release automatically resolves selected languages, pinned toolchains, generated bindings, assets, shaders, source documents, capability stripping, product projection, package layout, signatures, platform staging, and verification. Failures map to authored source and provide an actionable recovery path.

### The game is one codebase; language is an implementation property `PRJ-005` — *Normative*

Meridian game code is organized around **game concepts and ownership**, not language families. The normal source tree may freely look like:

```text
Code/
├── Player/
│   ├── Player.cs
│   └── Movement.rs
├── Enemies/
│   ├── Drone.cs
│   └── Navigation.rs
├── World/
│   ├── Door.cs
│   └── WeatherHooks.luau
└── UI/
    └── PauseMenu.cs
```

Meridian must never require this merely because multiple languages are selected:

```text
Code/
├── CSharp/
├── Rust/
├── Luau/
├── TypeScript/
└── Python/
```

A developer may choose language-oriented folders when that is useful, but Meridian does not impose them.

Consequences:

- source search, code navigation, references and the Asset/Project Browser treat the game as one logical code graph;
- language-service boundaries are implementation/tooling details;
- cross-language references have stable Meridian schema/interface identity rather than source-path magic;
- adding a language does not automatically restructure existing source;
- deleting a language removes its toolchain projection and dependencies without moving unrelated game code;
- build diagnostics resolve back to authored source paths and lines, never only into generated projection files;
- language names may appear in Advanced Build/Interop tooling, but ordinary gameplay organization should not require users to think in toolchains.

### Generated native toolchain projections are the preferred architecture `PRJ-006` — *Normative direction*

The preferred product model is that `project.meridian` plus authored code declarations form the high-level game-code authority, while Meridian deterministically projects the necessary native build/tooling metadata for each selected language into derived state, conceptually:

```text
.meridian/
└── generated/
    └── toolchains/
        ├── dotnet/
        │   ├── Game.csproj
        │   └── generated-bindings/
        ├── rust/
        │   ├── Cargo.toml
        │   ├── Cargo.lock / lock projection policy
        │   └── generated-bindings/
        └── <other selected language adapters>/
```

The exact physical filenames are not locked. The architectural properties are.

#### Mandatory projection properties

1. **Deterministic.** Identical source/configuration/toolchain inputs produce semantically identical projections.
2. **Disposable.** A projection can be deleted and regenerated without losing authored intent.
3. **Inspectable.** Experts can open generated manifests and see why entries exist.
4. **Source-mapped.** Diagnostics and debugger operations map back to authored game files and stable Meridian interface IDs.
5. **No hidden dependency invention.** Every native package/dependency must be explainable from project source or an explicit tool-owned transitive dependency.
6. **Lockfile-aware.** Reproducible native dependency resolution is retained; Meridian may not silently float package versions merely because a manifest is generated.
7. **Offline-capable.** Once required dependencies/toolchains are available locally, projection/build must not require a Meridian cloud service.
8. **IDE-capable.** Rider/VS Code/rust-analyzer and equivalent language tools need a stable way to consume the generated/native project graph.
9. **Failure-safe.** A projection generation failure leaves the previous valid projection/build available where safe and cannot rewrite authored source as a recovery trick.
10. **No proprietary Meridian compiler lock-in.** Game code remains ordinary language source.

#### What this intentionally supersedes

The earlier blanket statement "Cargo manifests and lockfiles remain authoritative for Rust" is refined for **game-project Rust**:

- Cargo remains the actual Rust package/compiler ecosystem and its resolved dependency graph/lock semantics remain authoritative at the Rust-toolchain boundary;
- however, the user-facing physical `Cargo.toml` need not be the top-level game architecture authority when Meridian can losslessly generate it from higher-level project intent;
- engine development itself remains a normal Cargo workspace and is not converted to this game-project projection model.

This distinction prevents a convenience rule for Meridian engine contributors from dictating the filesystem experience of every shipped game.

### Native-tooling escape hatch and R2 fallback are mandatory `PRJ-007` — *Normative*

PRJ-006 is allowed to remain the preferred direction only if prototypes prove it does not turn Meridian into a worse Cargo/MSBuild/package manager.

The qualification prototype must cover at least:

#### C#

- SDK-style compile-item discovery;
- NuGet package add/remove/update and lock/reproducibility behavior;
- analyzers/source generators;
- debugger launch/attach;
- Rider and VS Code project loading;
- project references where useful;
- generated Meridian bindings;
- build error/source mapping;
- self-contained and Native AOT publish qualification;
- one unsupported/difficult .NET feature with a clear fallback rather than silent omission.

#### Rust

- crates.io and git/path dependencies;
- feature flags;
- `build.rs`/proc-macro behavior under declared trust policy;
- rust-analyzer;
- debugger/source mapping;
- Cargo.lock semantics;
- native/library linking;
- generated Meridian bindings;
- target-specific dependencies;
- one advanced Cargo feature that tests whether projection is becoming leaky.

#### Polyglot

- C# calling a stable Meridian-exposed Rust service and vice versa where permitted;
- a source rename/move without broken generated identity;
- incremental rebuild where only affected toolchain graph nodes run;
- Play restart/hot-reload behavior;
- clean project checkout followed by projection regeneration;
- command-line/headless build without launching the GUI;
- complete deletion of `.meridian/generated/toolchains` followed by successful recovery.

#### Falsification rule

If Meridian must model a large and unstable percentage of Cargo/MSBuild semantics merely to keep normal language tooling functioning, **fall back to R2**:

> feature-oriented authored source tree + small visible native manifests.

That fallback is not considered a product failure. It is preferable to fragile magic.

R3-style explicit Meridian code modules may still be justified for reusable plugin/package boundaries, but cannot become required ceremony for an ordinary `Player.cs` or `movement.rs` file.

### Project root anti-complexity contract `PRJ-008` — *Normative*

A normal game checkout must answer four questions at a glance:

```text
What is the project?            project.meridian
Where is authored content?      Content/
Where is authored code?         Code/ (if any)
What can I delete/rebuild?      .meridian/ derived classes, with recovery exceptions clearly marked
```

The game root must not mirror engine subsystem names. The following are specifically forbidden as mandatory normal-game organization concepts:

- `Penumbra/`;
- `Cairn/`;
- `Isobar/`;
- `Torsant/`;
- `Basalt/`;
- `Alluvium/`;
- `Artus/`;
- `Wavefront/`;
- a directory per capability pack;
- a directory per language merely because the language is enabled;
- a directory per build stage;
- visible generated interface trees scattered beside source.

A subsystem may surface a source file/folder only when the *game itself* meaningfully authors content of that kind, and the source should still use game-facing language where practical.

### Build and Release are distinct product intents `PRJ-009` — *Normative*

`Play`, `Test`, `Build`, and `Release` are stable top-level intents over one typed build graph.

Internally Meridian distinguishes, where applicable:

```text
resolve
compile
import/cook
generate bindings
optimize
strip
stage
package
sign/notarize
verify
publish to an explicitly selected destination
```

These phases are observable jobs with provenance, cache identity, diagnostics, cancellation/retry semantics, and artifact lineage. They are not mandatory buttons in the normal editor.

A Build result is a local runnable/staged product. A Release result is an immutable release record plus verified artifacts and optional provider-specific staging/publication state. Build may be performed repeatedly without creating a release. Release may consume an already verified Build when identity matches exactly.

### Cross-system consequences

#### DAT / Asset Catalog

- Content source paths remain human-readable but are never sole persistent identity.
- Asset type/category search remains semantic and independent of physical folders.
- cooked artifacts do not appear in `Content/`.

#### Polyglot/GAM

- one neutral interface schema mediates durable cross-language APIs;
- language adapters consume the same lifecycle, save, input, command and diagnostics contracts;
- the project tree does not encode runtime scheduling order.

#### Build

- one dependency DAG spans all selected language projections and asset/render/package stages;
- generated native manifests enter BuildId/provenance identity;
- cache hits must not require generated files to pollute the source root.

#### VCS / MVS

- authored project/code/content remain normal version-controlled files;
- derived toolchain projections are ignored by default unless a future evidence gate proves a particular native lock artifact must be committed;
- MVS semantic status should distinguish authored changes from rebuildable generated changes.

#### Editor

- project creation should show a small meaningful tree immediately;
- Advanced Project Structure can reveal generated projections, resolved packages and ownership without making those ordinary folders;
- command/search indexes both authored files and relevant generated diagnostics, but authored results rank above generated projections for normal navigation.

#### Release/package

- the game source tree places no constraint on the shipped install tree;
- the built artifact is a separate product architecture, defined next.
